en: *Chuiyu Ji* (Record of the Bequeathed Benefits), a Brief Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyuan of Qiandeng.
The commentary on the *Vimalakīrti* is divided into two parts: First, the Preface, which has two sub-sections: first, the preface written by Liang Su; second, [the preface] by Jingxi.
Preface. The first section has two parts:
first, the preface to the title.
Preface to the Abridged Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra Vimalakīrti, when fully expressed, is called Vimalakīrti; in this language, it means "Pure Name.
"Pure" refers to the True Body (dharmakāya), and "Name" refers to the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya).
"Truth" (*zhen*) refers to the principle realized; "response" (*ying*) refers to the body manifested.
"Sūtra" (*jing*) is explained as "dharma" and "permanence.
As for dharma, it is that upon which all capacities of beings rely; as for permanence, it is that which is not altered by even a hundred kings.
This work explains the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) and elucidates his transformative teachings; therefore, it is called the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
As for the term "Brief Commentary" (*Lüeshù*), it is so named in contrast to the extensive version.
It is called a "Brief Commentary" because it prunes away the profuse and the weeds while extracting the essential points.
"Preface" (*xu*) means "to narrate. It describes the reasons for Jingxi’s abridgments as well as the intent behind the Holy Master’s establishment of the teaching; hence it is called a "preface.
Furthermore, these six characters of the title involve four layers of subject and object:
first, *Vimalakīrti* is that which is explained (*suōquán*), while the "sūtra" is that which explains (*néngquán*); this refers to Vimalakīrti.
Second, the "upper" refers to that which is to be understood, while the "commentary" (*shu*) is that which understands; this terminology belongs to the wise.
Third, the "commentary" is that which is abridged, and "abridgment" (*lue*) is that which performs the abridgment; this belongs to Jingxi.
Fourth: All that has been enumerated above constitutes the "Preface" (xu), which is itself the means of introduction; this is according to Liang Su.

Since one takes the expressed meaning (*saṃprakāśita-artha*) as the specific name of the Sūtra, one likewise takes the explained meaning (*vyākhyāta-artha*) as the specific title of the Commentary (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, the name is received by the means of abbreviation (*saṃkṣepa*) from that which is abbreviated.

Although the detailed divisions are thus, if one summarizes and encompasses them as a whole, the five characters above are simply alternative names for the "Preface" (xu), distinguishing it from other prefaces;
the single character "Preface" (xu) itself is the general name.
Next is the description of the author’s title. Regarding the phrase "disciple" (*ménrén*): it is a term used for a student.
Having received the Way from Jingxi, he composed this preface on behalf of Jingxi and referred to himself as a "disciple."

Regarding the Hanlin: Under the Han system, the Secretaries of the Department of State Affairs (Shangshu Lang) were responsible for composing literary works. They rose early to take turns on night duty within the Tai (Palace) at the Jianli Gate. They were provided with covers made of blue silk or white damask, or brocade, as well as curtains, mats, and rugs; furthermore, the Grand Cook’s Office supplied them with meals throughout the mid-autumn period.
This was roughly similar to the current system of the Hanlin Academy, yet the responsibilities it held were no light matter.

The *Hanyin Tiyao* states: "In the Tang dynasty, following the precedents of the Liang and Chen dynasties, there were six Secretaries of the Chancellery (*zhongshu sheren*) who specialized in drafting imperial decrees and inquiries; although these were termed 'prohibitions' and 'palace matters,' they were still not considered strictly confidential."
Therefore, Wen Daye, Wei Zheng, Li Baiyao, Cen Wenben, Chu Suiliang, Xu Jingzong, and Shangguan Yi were occasionally summoned to draft imperial edicts, yet they had not yet received official titles.

After the Qianfeng era, they were first called Northern Gate Academicians (*beimen xueshi*). Liu Yizhi, Liu Weizhi, Zhou Simao, Yuan Wansheng, and Fan Lübing served in this capacity; during the Zetian reign, Su Wei and Wei Chengqing held these posts.
Later, the title was changed to Hanlin Dazhao (Imperial Scribe), held successively by Zhang Yue, Lu Jian, Zhang Jiuling, and Xu Anzhen. It was further changed to Hanlin Gongfeng (Imperial Attendant);
in the twenty-sixth year of the Kaiyuan era, Liu Qianguang and Zhang Ju served as Academicians, at which time the Xueshiyuan (Academy of Academicians) was first established as a separate institution.

The number of scholars was not fixed; they were all filled by officials from other posts, ranging from the lowest rank of Proofreader (xiàoshūláng) up to the various Ministers of State (shàngshū). All such individuals were eligible to serve as them.

Once they had entered, they were separated from the official ranks; they were not subject to the *li-si* (daily attendance) nor bound by the regular court sessions (*chang-can*). Serving in office for three years constituted a full term. Those appointed as *Buque* (Censor for Omissions) were charged with providing ritual service and offering admonitions.
The *Shi* says, "When there was a deficiency in the duties of the Chancellor, it was Zhong Shanfu who filled it.
In the Imperial Court, this title was changed to "Director of Remonstrance" (*Sikan*).

Regarding the term "holding the office of Right Supplementary Deficiency" (*shou you buque*): when one's rank is high but the office is low, one is said to be "acting" (*xing*); when one's rank is low but the office is high, one is said to be "holding" (*shou*); when rank and office are of equal grade, the terms "acting" or "holding" are not used.
Now, because this is a brief mention, there is no formal rank.
Liang Su, whose courtesy name was Jingzhi, wrote in the "Preface to the Rhapsody on Passing Through My Old Garden": "I was eight years old when it was the Xinchou year of the Shangyuan era."

He entered Luoyang as a fugitive; the region between the Three Rivers was plunged into great turmoil and suffering. Consequently, he fled eastward and traveled through Wu and Yue, wandering among the narrow passes for nearly twenty years.
Upon the Emperor’s accession to the throne, he attended the capital in accordance with an imperial decree.
The following summer, he was appointed as a Proofreader (xiàoshū láng) at the Eastern Palace.
According to the *Yùnlì*, "In the sixth year of Emperor Dēngzōng’s Zhēnyuán era, the year Gēngwǔ, Liáng Sù served as a Court Rectifier (bǔquè)."

The *Preface to the Collected Works of Lord Cui Gongliang* states: "The Lord followed the teachings of Śākyamuni from an early age; his understanding of their principles was innate, and he composed writings with this as his sole purpose."

In conversation and discourse, as well as in laughter and jest, he was constantly engaged in mutual refinement; his mind was fixed upon the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), and thus his expositions on the teachings of Śākya were preeminent for their precision and breadth.
Indeed, he was the herald for the Buddha’s doctrine and its manifestation; as the imperial court esteemed virtue, he was appointed as the Tutor to the Crown Prince.
As the state prizes historical records, you were appointed as a member of the Historiography Institute;
as the court seeks to cultivate the sovereign’s governance through refined composition, you were appointed as a Hanlin Academician.
When he has held all three offices concurrently, his position at court cannot be considered unsuccessful.
Having reached an age beyond forty, with the scholarly community honoring him, he may not be said to have lacked longevity when compared to those such as Yan Hui or Huang Zhongtu.

Li Ao’s “Preface to the Rhapsody on Feeling Gratitude for a Comrade-in-Arms” states: “In the ninth year of the Zhenyuan era, I, Ao, first entered the service of the provincial government as a tribute candidate.
In the ninth month of that year, carrying a single manuscript of my writings, I went to call upon Mr. Liang of Anding, who served as Right Assistant in the Palace Library.”
At that time, the reputation of the Lord of Liang filled the world; those who sought advancement by presenting their compositions came to the gate of the Lord of Liang every day without fail.

When Lord Liang recognized my faults, and we had already met, he subsequently established with me the way of mutual understanding; he claimed that I had attained the lingering spirit of the ancient texts, hoping that my name would remain imperishable throughout eternity, and promising to polish and fan me into brilliance.
At first, I thought he was merely advancing his own interests, and I did not consider it particularly fortunate.
In the eleventh month, Lord Liang fell ill and passed away; subsequently, as I moved among my friends and high officials, they would often say:
"I have already had my name recorded by you for the sake of Liang Jiu, the Director of the Bureau of Supplements."
By this, we know that Lord Liang passed away in the eleventh month of the ninth year of the Zhenyuan era.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) of our Imperial Court states: "Although there were many high-ranking officials among the disciples of Jingxi, the only one who truly attained his Way was the Academician Liang Su."
The *Shijing* says, "The magpie has built its nest; the dove dwells within it.
Does this not refer to Prince Liang’s profound penetration into the inner sanctum of the Buddha’s principles?

He once edited and determined the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) into six fascicles and composed a single fascicle of the *Tong li* (General Principles) to follow it, much like Zheng Xufu’s *Lüe li* (Brief Examples) appended to his commentary on the *Yi jing*.
When this preface was being composed, Master Liang was residing in Yue.

Part Three: The Preface, in two sections: First, a brief preface outlining the fundamental principles, in two sections: 1. A brief preface outlining the fundamental principles; 2. [The second section].
First, the transmission of the Dharma by the wise consists of two parts.
First, clarifying that three matters are mutually dependent:
the Sage does not arise without the Path; the Path is not clarified without the Teaching; and the Teaching is not practiced without people. These three depend upon one another to exist.
The *Baïhûtōng* says: "What is a sage (*shèngrén*)? 'Sage' means penetration, the Way, and sound.

Because the Way penetrates all things without exception, his clarity illuminates all things without exception, and he understands the inner state of others upon hearing their voices, he is called a sage."
Now, "sage" (ārya) refers to realization; one is called a sage because of severing delusions and realizing the principle.
The Way is precisely the principle; because one becomes a sage by realizing the principle, it is for this reason that the Tathāgata attained the Way at the site of tranquility (Śītavane).

"The Way is not clarified without teaching": although the principle is beyond words, one awakens to the principle by means of words; this is why Vimalakīrti bestowed his teachings upon Vaiśālī. "Teaching does not circulate without people":
for the teaching to be transmitted to future generations, it cannot spread without the Four Reliances; this is why Zhiyi composed his commentaries at Tiantai.
These three refer to principle (li), teaching (jiao), and person (ren).
This means that by awakening to principle one becomes a sage; one awakens to principle through the teaching; and the transmission of the teaching must necessarily depend on persons.
Because these three matters are mutually dependent, they are said to abide in mutual reliance.
Second, specifically indicating that people can transmit the Way, in two parts:
first, Vimalakīrti’s bestowal of instruction.
The Way has its great and small, its provisional and real; thus, Vimalakīrti brought about transformation while remaining a layman.

The ultimate Way is one, yet it varies according to the capacities of beings. Consequently, there is a distinction between the True and the Mean within principle: those with the capacities of the *āgama* (Tripitaka) and *vaipulya* (Shared) teachings perceive only the provisional principle of emptiness, whereas those with the capacities of the *pratyekabuddha* (Distinct) and *bodhisattva* (Complete) teachings perceive the real principle of the Middle Way.
The Lesser [Vehicle] conceals the principle, while the Greater [Vehicle] encompasses the three teachings.

Since capacities and conditions are not uniform and the realization of the Way is not consistent, Vimalakīrti manifested in the body of a layman to praise the greatness of the three teachings and refute the smallness of the Tripiṭaka; he extolled the perfect reality and censured the partial expedient, intending thereby to cause those who cling to the small to aspire toward the great, and to lead them from the expedient into the real.
II. The Transmission of the Teachings by the Wise Master (Jizang) has two parts:
first, the composition of commentaries (*śāstra*) to expound the sutras.
Since individuals vary in their spiritual capacity—whether saintly or ordinary, profound or shallow—the Wise Master initiated the Dharma by relying on the *Chuyi* (The Initial Basis).

The person is precisely the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*). The first reliance pertains to the stage of the worthy (*ārya-pudgala*), and is thus shallow; the latter three reliances pertain to the stage of the noble (*ārya*), and are thus deep. All four reliances are capable of practicing the teaching.
Now, the Wise One (Chih-i), because the first reliance pertains to the stage of the worthy, composed a commentary to elucidate the sutras and open up the teachings.

The five stages and the six faculties constitute the first reliance; the ten abidings are the second reliance; the ten practices and the ten transferences are called the third reliance; and the ten grounds are the fourth reliance.
All are termed "reliances" because they possess internal dharmas that can serve as a basis for humans and devas.
Second, the benefit for those in the final age:

thereafter, by means of words one discards words, and by means of the image one forgets the image, enabling later students to attain the path of the true and correct and to traverse the gateway of the Way and its meaning.

However, while the Buddha’s assembly received the Way through Vimalakīrti, it was after his parinirvāṇa that they benefited from its merit due to the power of the Wise One; this commentary clarifies the intent of the sūtra so as to enable people to attain understanding.
Because liberation is achieved through words, it is said that "one uses words to dispel words.
Because one contemplates the true reality of the body, it is said that "one forgets the image upon encountering the image.

The terms "words" and "images" originate from the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*); here they are applied by dividing them according to the discourse on the body, so as not to let the literal phrasing obstruct the intended meaning.
The *Zhouyi lueli* states: "Words are the means by which images are clarified; once the image is grasped, one forgets the words.
Images are the means by which the intended meaning is preserved; once the meaning is grasped, one forgets the images."

Regarding the phrase "to enable those of later generations," *bi* (俾) means "to cause" or "to enable. It signifies that by causing the students of future generations to seek out the meanings of the commentaries and penetrate the purport of the sutras, they may attain the path of correct and true exposition and enter the gate of the principles of the Vaipulya (Universal) Way.
The *Yi* says, "When one's nature is perfected and preserved in its constant existence, it is the gateway to the Way and righteousness.
Second, the manifestation of Jingxi’s ancestral transmission:
to take as an ancestor and transmit his teachings depends upon the individual.
"Ancestral" (*zu*) means "model" (*fa*).
The *Wenxuan* states, "the soil that constitutes the ancestral foundation," with the commentary noting, "'Ancestral' means 'model.
The person referred to is Jingxi.
The *Yi* says, "To divine and clarify it depends upon the person. II.
An extensive exposition of the causes and conditions, in two parts: A.
The primary exposition of the causes and conditions, in two parts: [subsequent sections follow].
First, the formal narration of Jingxi’s ancestral transmission, in two parts:
first, clarifying that he received the essential intent of the lineage, in two parts:
first, a brief eulogy.

The great bhikṣu Zhanran of Tiantai compiled the dharma-lineage of the Master Zhiyi and explored the subtle mysteries of the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra; he unified the study of written texts and brought all things back to the profound abyss of liberation.
Regarding the term "Great Bhikṣu," "Great" (Dai) is a word used for praise and commendation.
When there are those in the world who style themselves "Great Śramaṇas," is this not merely a loss of propriety born of self-conceit, but also the fault of being unlearned and ignorant?
"Zuǎn" means to collect.
"Yìn" means to succeed.
"Tàn" means to take up.
"Ze" means profound.
"Vaiśālī" is translated here as "Extensive Splendor"; this sutra was preached in the city of Vaiśālī.
"Yuan" means ocean.
The *Wenxuan* states, "Profound as the deep abyss," with the commentary noting, "The deep abyss is the ocean.

This is because Jingxi, inheriting the doctrinal gates of Tiantai, sought the purport of this sutra; thus, he was able to realize that the superficial matters of words and letters are themselves the profound principle of liberation.
Second, the detailed exposition.

It is said that when the Great Master Zhiyi of old expounded this sutra, he fully elucidated the meanings of the partial and the perfect, the sudden and the gradual; he exhausted the essence of the Vaipulya and the "fresh butter" (Sutras); its purport was profound and its Way subtle.

The subtle words are present herein; by means of this, one is rendered free from delusion. Therefore, he constantly elucidates the teachings outwardly and clarifies his illumination inwardly, such that all students who gaze upon the shore find it like returning home.
Regarding the exposition of this sutra, it refers to the composition of the commentary at the request of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty.
As for the inclusion of the partial, the complete, and so forth, this is because the sutra critiques the partial and the gradual, and explains all four teachings.
Regarding "fresh butter" (*navanīta*): in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha enumerates five flavors as a metaphor for the teachings of his entire lifetime.

The milk produced from the cow symbolizes the Buddha’s initial teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*; the curd produced from the milk symbolizes the Deer Park; the fresh butter produced from the curd symbolizes the *Vaipulya* (or *Vaipulya-sūtras*); the clarified butter produced from the fresh butter symbolizes the *Prajñāpāramitā*; and the ghee produced from the clarified butter symbolizes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
The meaning of this passage is as follows: he praises the profound and far-reaching intent of the commentary’s text and the subtle and refined nature of its principles.
"Subtle words" refers to the fact that the commentary consists of such refined and subtle discourse.
It exists in the world, and thus it is said to "be here. "Here" (茲) means this.
Regarding "employing this to eliminate delusion":

by employing these subtle words, one cultivates the methods of contemplation within and instructs those who are ignorant without; in both self-cultivation and transforming others, there will certainly be no doubt or confusion.
To externally propagate its teachings is to expound them for the sake of transforming others;
to internally clarify its illumination is to personally cultivate contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
When the water of the mind is clear and still, the reflection of the jewel appears; hence it is called "clarifying illumination."
Furthermore, "zhào" (照) means clarity;
"chéng" (澄) means stillness.
The phrase "all those below" clarifies that the student purifies themselves and returns to Jingxi as if returning to their own home.
The edge of water is called its "shore.
Second, [this section] shows the reasons and basis for the deletions and abridgments.
He once said to his disciples:
The Way described by the Patriarchs is most manifest; yet those who favor brevity may find it overly prolix, while those who delight in the subtle may neglect its grosser aspects.
I wish to build upon this foundation to extend their teaching, and to prune and refine it so as to preserve its essentials.
"What do you think?
The disciple-monks then performed a prostration and made their request.
The Duke thereupon edited the refined language and compiled it into ten fascicles; he did not deviate from the original principles, and its meaning became even more clear.
Circulating together with the preceding section, it is titled the *Jingming lüeshu* (Abridged Commentary on the Vimalakīrti).

Its teachings were highly renowned; specifically, the commentary on the title of the sutra consists of six fascicles titled "Xuan" (Profound), while the commentary on the main text of the sutra consists of twenty-eight fascicles titled "Wen" (Text). Since the total commentaries amount to thirty-four fascicles, they are said to be very renowned.
Other editions read "extremely great" (shèndà), which is also acceptable.
The term "extremely great" originates from the *I Ching* (*Zhouyi*).
The term "extremely prominent" (shènzhù) originates from the *Wenxuan*.
Yet, his fondness for the inferior was the fault of producing an overly expansive commentary.
"Fondness" (shì) means greed;
"simplification" (jiǎn) means brevity.
I wish to simplify it, intending to delete and abridge.
Those who follow this approach do so by taking the existing commentary as a basis to compose a text that extends the teachings of the Sūtra; it is not a separate composition.
"To prune and edit" means to excise and trim away redundant and chaotic expressions in order to preserve their essential and concise teachings.
Thus, Jingxi’s own preface states: "That which carries the meaning must be preserved; where the words are prolix, they shall be trimmed."
"What is it like? means to raise a matter to inquire whether it may be so or not.
As for the disciples below, since their sentiments were already satisfied, they collectively made this request.
Regarding the excision of refined expressions, "excision" has two meanings:
"First, to excise; second, to extract.
Now, it is said that from within the extensive commentary, the pure words have been extracted and compiled as a separate work.
Although the text is abbreviated, the categories of meaning remain unchanged; therefore, it is said that the original principles are not lost."
Since the redundant phrasing has been excised, the essential meaning becomes even more evident; thus it is said that "its meaning is now perfectly clear.
This follows from the previous section, clarifying that Jingxi merely trimmed away superfluous words while not discarding the original commentary.
In contrast to the old version, the designation "extensive" and "abbreviated" arose for the new version.

The intention was that those who prefer extensiveness should consult the old version, while those who prefer brevity should follow the new; thus, they were circulated alongside the preceding sections so that each might follow their own preference.
"Xié" (偕) means "equal.
Second, a general clarification of the great principles of establishing the teaching, in two parts:
first, clarifying the establishment of the teaching according to capacities.
Originally, the Sage perceived that the capacities for the generation of life are not uniform; therefore, he employed the four teachings and the five flavors of the sutras to interweave them.
He also perceived that the expansion and contraction of the myriad dharmas are not distinct; therefore, he employed the One Way and the One Vehicle to harmonize and perfect them.
In this passage, it is first clarified that the Sage’s observation of capacities is not uniform.
"The Sage" refers to the Buddha.
"All beings" (shengsheng) refers to the multitude of living beings; it is equivalent to saying "every person."

Nevertheless, all sentient beings are fundamentally endowed with the one path, which is equal and without distinction; it is only due to the depth or shallowness of their habitual conditioning that there arise differences in terms of provisional versus ultimate, or sharp versus dull faculties—hence, they are said to be "not uniform."

Therefore, by employing this [passage], it is clarified that the Buddha accords with the capacities of sentient beings; thus, there is the teaching of a single lifetime (*ekayuga-dharma*), which begins with the ripening through the four flavors and concludes with the ultimate convergence at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The phrase "the four teachings are woven as warp" clarifies the teaching of the four flavors (*catur-rasa*).

The five flavors discussed vertically are like the warp of a fabric, while the four teachings distinguished horizontally are like the woof; this is why there are two teachings at the Avataṃsaka, only one at the Deer Park, all four at the Vaipulya, and only three at the Prajñāpāramitā.
The capacities of sentient beings are not uniform; although there are actually four flavors, they are collectively enumerated as five.
The following section clarifies the teachings of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Regarding the terms "relaxation" (*chi*) and "tension" (*zhang*), "relaxation" refers to the opposite [of tension].
The *Book of Rites* states: "Tension and relaxation constitute the way of the Kings Wen and Wu. The commentary notes: "This uses the bow and crossbow as a metaphor for human beings.
If a bow or crossbow is kept constantly drawn, its strength will be severed; if it is left constantly slack, its form will be lost."
The present mention of "relaxation and tension" is like "abandonment and flourishing.
Since the nature of all phenomena—both arising and ceasing—is one and the same, it is said they are not different.

However, prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the capacities of sentient beings were uneven and they were not yet capable of receiving this teaching; now that their karmic conditions have matured, both the partial (Hīnayāna) and the complete (Mahāyāna) paths return to the same source, which is why it is said they are "converged and perfected."
Second, clarifying the intent behind establishing the teachings, in two parts:
first, clarifying the dual distinction between the ancient and the modern.
Thus, because the Sage manifests benefits in accordance with responsive conditions, his teachings cannot help but differ.
The worthy and wise, moved by resonance, establish sincerity; thus their work cannot but be transmitted.
The Buddha, abiding in the state of fruition through supreme virtue, is fit for sentient beings to behold; therefore, it is said that he is "to be seen with benefit."
The *Yi* says: "The flying dragon is in the heavens; it is advantageous to see the great man.
That there must be no discrepancy [in our teaching] is because we follow the opportune conditions of beings; thus, there are distinctions between the five periods and the four teachings.
"Virtuous and wise" refers to those who possess discernment.

"Establishing sincerity through resonance" means that, because they were moved by the spiritual resonance of Vimalakīrti’s teaching, they composed the words of this commentary to further elucidate its essential meaning.
The *Yi* says, "Cultivate one's speech and establish sincerity; this is how one dwells in their vocation.
It was impossible not to transmit [this work], for its benefits extend even to the final age; thus, its commentaries and meanings must necessarily be passed down.
"Philosophy (zhe)" means wisdom.
Second, it clarifies that responding to capacities is of one principle.

When observing their respective inspirations, we see that whether it be Vimalakīrti at Vaiśālī or Tiantai [Zhiyi], whether it be the silence of the Buddha or the establishment of words by the patriarchs—though their stages differ and their breadth or brevity varies according to what is appropriate—the underlying intent remains the same.
As for responding to opportunities to provide instruction, the underlying principle is one and the same.
Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī, while Zhiyi established his words at Tiantai.
"Establishing words" refers to the composition of commentaries.

In the *Zuozhuan*, Mu Shu said: "The highest excellence lies in establishing one's virtue; next is establishing one's achievements; and next is establishing one's words. These are what are called 'imperishable.'"
Regarding the difference in their stages: Vimalakīrti is a sage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), while Zhìzhě is a worthy of the five grades.
Regarding the difference between the extensive and the concise, it encompasses two meanings:
first, to remain silent is "concise," while to establish words is "extensive."
Second, [it is said that] Jingxi’s [commentary] is concise while Zhiyi’s is extensive;

these differences exist because both respond to the specific capacities of sentient beings. However, regarding their benefit to all things, they are in fact no different; thus, the conclusion states, "As for responding to capacities," and so forth.
"Kui" means to measure.
Second, the self-humbling description of intent, in two parts:
first, the formal expression of humility.

Xu once received the scriptures from the Master’s gate and pursued the Way in the academy of righteousness; though he could not reach the heights of his profound veneration, he found it impossible to exhaust his admiration, and thus composed this preface to set forth the reasons for the Master’s literary works in written words.
"Those who received the scriptures at the gate of the Master" refers to those who received the meaning of the scriptures from the school of Jingxi.

Regarding "none could reach [the depths]," this alludes to Yan Yuan’s praise of the Master in the *Analects*: "The more I looked up to him, the higher he seemed; the more I drilled into him, the firmer he proved. Hence, it is said that none could reach [the limit].
Regarding the insufficiency of mere sighs and exclamations, the *Preface to the Mao Shih* states: "When sighs and exclamations are insufficient, one therefore chants and sings.

Now, the Lord of Liang, having received the scriptures and grasped their essential meaning, and further having beheld the edited and abridged texts of Jingxi, found that sighs and exclamations were insufficient; thus, he composed this preface to narrate these matters and set them down in literary form.
2. Recording the Year and Season.
The year in which this commentary was completed was the Jiachen year, during the summer when our Master returned from Jinling to Fulong.
Jiachen corresponds to the second year of the Guangde era of the Tang dynasty Emperor Daizong.
Jinling is the name of a commandery located in Changzhou.
Fulong is located in Tiantai.
Shen Yong’s *Mountains Record* states: "Walking two hundred paces south from Xiu Chan Temple, there is a flat rock, level and smooth as if carved."
"According to ancient tradition, the Buddha once emitted light here; therefore, it is named Fulong (Buddha’s Ridge).
That summer, Jingxi resided at Xiuchan Temple.
II. Jingxi’s own preface, in two parts:
First, the title.

Since this is an autocommentary, the author’s name should not be appended; it is like Kong Anguo’s commentary on the *Shangshu*, Du Yuankai’s collected commentary on the *Chunqiu*, or He Yan’s collected commentary on the *Lunyu*—all of which include self-composed prefaces yet none record the authors’ names.
Given the vast learning of Jingxi [Zhiyi], he surely followed the precedent of former masters; thus, all ancient editions lack the author’s name.
Any such attribution found in modern editions was added arbitrarily by later generations.
II. The Main Text, in two parts:
First, the Prologue to the Composition of the Commentary.
Regarding "Emperor Yang of the Sui": the Sui dynasty had three sovereigns, namely Gaozu, Emperor Wen, and Emperor Yang.
After Emperor Gong abdicated to the Tang dynasty,
Gaozu’s father— known posthumously as Zhong, General of the Chariot and Cavalry of Zhou, and enfeoffed as the Duke of Sui—
was honored with the title Emperor Wuyuan after Emperor Wen had received the abdication from Zhou and established the state name as the Great Sui.
"Yang" (Yǎng) is a posthumous title (*shìhào*); the *Shìfǎ* (Methods of Posthumous Titles) states: "One who defies Heaven and oppresses the people is called Yang.
As for "Emperor" (*dì*), the *Báihùtōng* says: "One whose virtue accords with Heaven and Earth is titled Emperor."
Question:
Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty and Emperor Houzhu of the Chen dynasty both received instruction from the Tiantai school; why did they both lose their way and forfeit their kingdoms?
Could this perhaps be the fault of the Great Master?
Answer:

From beginning with what is good to ending in calamity, even to the point of losing one’s state—if one simply receives the teacher’s instruction and practices it without fail—how could such a thing come to pass?
Thus, the *Book of Documents* says: "Only the madman who can maintain mindfulness becomes a sage; only the sage who lacks mindfulness becomes mad."
Therefore, the nature of the person of middle capacity must be carefully guarded; this is not the case for those of superior wisdom.
Thus it is said: "To have a beginning and an end—this belongs only to the sage."
Therefore, since the practice lies with the disciple, how can one blame the teacher?
In the past, Li Si studied Confucianism under Xunzi, and Yuan Song studied Buddhism under the nameless master.

Yet when Li Si served as Chancellor of Qin, he buried the scholars alive and burned the books; and when Yuan Song assisted the Zhou dynasty, he suppressed the Śākya teachings and destroyed the Buddha. How could the fault be attributed to their teachers?

Furthermore, even though the sages Yao, Shun, and the Duke of Zhou were so holy, their sons were as unworthy as Dan Zhu and Shang Jun, and their younger brothers were as unkind as Guan Shu and Cai Shu; was it not that the instruction of Yao, Shun, and the Duke of Zhou had failed to reach them?
Wen Zhongzi said: "The flourishing of the Odes and the Documents led to the destruction of Qin; this was not the fault of Confucius.
The growth of the doctrine of emptiness and mystery led to the chaos of Jin; this was not the fault of Lao Dan."
"The state of Liang was endangered because its rulers practiced fasting and celibacy; this was not the fault of Śākyamuni.
By this it is made clear that the lack of virtue in Emperor Yang of Sui and the reckless indulgence of the Later Zhou ruler were not the fault of the wise [Buddha].

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they may manifest the absence of the Way or manifest the presence of the Way. Manifesting the absence of the Way serves as a warning for the hundred kings, causing them to distance themselves from evil;
manifesting the presence of the Way serves as a model for the hundred kings, causing them to transform toward goodness.
Such being the case, his actions accorded with the circumstances and were in accordance with principle; how could they possibly be reached by mere words?
Emperor Yang’s taboo name was Guang; he reigned for eleven years, lived to the age of fifty-nine, and his reign era was Daye.

Regarding the phrase "the Imperial Edict" (*chìwén*) and so forth: as for an "edict" (*chì*), the *Wénxīn diáolóng* states: "At the beginning of the Han dynasty, the protocols were established with four categories:

first, the *cèshū*; second, the *zhìshū*; third, the *zhàoshū*; and fourth, the *jièchì*. The *jièchì* was used to admonish the provinces and commanderies; the *zhàoshū* to proclaim to the various officials; the *zhìshū* to issue amnesties and decrees; and the *cèshū* to confer titles upon princes and marquises."
"Ce" means to select;
"zhi" means to regulate;
and "zhao" means to proclaim.
"Chì (勅) means 'correctness' (*zhèng*).
The *Yāoyán* says: 'Chì means correctness; it refers to the issue of royal edicts being promulgated downward to rectify the ministers, such that none dare to disobey.'"
Generally speaking, as imperial edicts and decrees were of the same nature, it was during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty that yellow paper first began to be used for writing edicts and decrees.
Reaching the second year of the Shangyuan era of Emperor Gaozong, an edict was issued stating:

"Since edicts and decrees, once implemented, serve as permanent models, the white paper currently used has frequently suffered from insect damage. Henceforth, all documents issued by the Department of State Affairs (Shangshu Sheng) to the empire shall be written on yellow paper."
"Guoqing" is the name of the monastery.

As for the "Hundred Records," it refers to the compilation by Zhangan of one hundred entries—including the monastic rules and rituals established during the Master’s lifetime, imperial edicts, and correspondence from ministers and officials—organized into five fascicles. It is titled the "Guoqing Hundred Records" because it is named after the monastery.
When this commentary was compiled, Emperor Yang was still the Prince of Jin; it was only after the Great Master’s passing that he ascended the throne.
Since the account follows the later chronology, it refers to Emperor Yang and the imperial edict.

According to the Han system, the Son of Heaven was styled as "Chì" (Imperial Decree); the Empress and the Crown Prince were styled as "Lìng" (Edict); and the various princes were styled as "Jiào" (Instruction).
Below the term "shìzhě" (attendant), it refers to those who provide personal service, who are called "shìzhě."
Since the Great Master entered *nirvāṇa*, the work concludes only with the "Chapter on the Buddha-way," which was in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era.
The *Biézhuan* states: "Emperor Yang, facing the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* commentary left behind by the Master, made this vow:

'In the past, though I personally attended upon the Master’s countenance, I did not have the opportunity to seek his resolution; now that I receive his final instructions, by what means can I attain awakening?'"
He prayed, "May your profound and compassionate instruction allow me to generate understanding as I examine the text.
That night, he was moved by a dream: a multitude of monks gathered at the pavilion, and the King himself expounded the meaning and resolved difficult points with fluency.
He saw his former teacher fly through the air and arrive; seven precious jewels poured forth, shimmering brilliantly within the pavilion, before flying away again.
"From this, he attained awakening.
Furthermore, the *Biézhuàn* (Separate Biography) states: "Throughout his life, the Great Master’s lectures and expositions were not recorded in formal commentaries (*zhangshu*).
He only composed the *Jìngmíng Shū* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) by imperial decree, reaching twenty-eight fascicles at the point of the 'Buddha-Dharma' Chapter (*Fódào Pǐn*)."
The latter part consists of six chapters: "The Gate of Non-duality," "The Fragrant Accumulation," "The Practice of Bodhisattvas," "The Land of Akṣobhya Buddha," "Dharma Offerings," and "Entrustment."
“Zhang’an” is the name of a place; his secular name was Guanding.
Because later scholars held him in high esteem, they referred to him by the name of his birthplace.

Yet, as the Great Master’s eloquence flowed like clouds and rained down like dew, he alone among those capable of receiving and memorizing it was Zhang’an; thus, all the teachings of the various sections were compiled and refined by Zhang’an.
2. Regarding the section beginning with "The first text," the causes and conditions are abbreviated in two parts:
first, the junior students found the original too prolix.
"Zisu" (black and white) refers to the monastic and the lay.
In the Western lands (India), monastic robes are dyed [black], while secular clothing is white; hence the terms "dark" (*zī*) and "white" (*sù*).
In this region (China), the sixth sense-base (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) is considered "mysterious" (*xuán*), and the seventh sense-base is considered "dark" (*zī*); yet "dark" is actually black in color.

The robes worn by the sons of the Śākya are dyed with colors that have been altered; they are neither the five primary colors nor the secondary colors. Because these altered colors closely resemble black, they are called "black robes" (zhīyī), though in reality they are not black.

Regarding the section beginning with "Profound Insight" (*shanjian*): the three contemplations and four teachings discussed in this commentary are profound in intent and elevated in diction; therefore, they are not what those of shallow understanding prefer.
Regarding the section beginning with "But it says": although all hold them in admiration, everyone suffers from their prolixity and breadth.
2. Regarding the section beginning with "Therefore, I have ventured" (*gu qie*), Jingxi has made three types of deletions and abbreviations:
first, he indicates the general principles of his editorial revisions.
*Qie* (ventured) means "exclusively" or "solely."
The *shū* (commentary) was compiled by an attendant; hence it says, "its record.
The phrase "to select and omit" indicates its general principles (*fánlì*).
In the section following "carrying the meaning," the first sentence represents what is selected, and the second sentence represents what is omitted.
The phrase "retaining the old" below indicates the merits of this abridged commentary.
Since it preserves the underlying meaning, the literary style of the original commentary remains intact without alteration.
"Former Master" refers to Zhiyi.
Second, from "However, [he himself]" onwards, it reveals the master's hidden grace.
"Ran" (然) is the name of Jingxi.

Among the eminent monks of antiquity who composed autobiographical accounts, many referred to themselves by a single character; as Sengyou states in the "Preface" to the *Hongming ji*: "I, You, am a student of the final dharma."
Regarding the *Nirvāṇa-yuanqi*, Zhiyan (Zhang’an) describes it in his own preface as the "Chapter on Stalling at the Summit" (*Dingzhaji yuzhang*).
The character *sheng* means "to look.
This refers to looking back upon one’s own ignorance and lack of talent; although he wished to condense and omit [the text], he feared that he might lose the Master’s original standards.
"Yuan" means the fundamental.
"Gui" refers to the compass and square.
The *Mencius* says: "A master craftsman instructs others by means of the compass and square."
"Once" (*cháng*) means "formerly.
"Tomb-chamber" (*féntáng*) refers to the site of the Great Master’s stupa; in Sanskrit it is called *stūpa*, which here is translated as "square mound.
The *Dāngōng* states: "In antiquity, there were graves but no mounds."
"Now, as for me, Qiu, I am a man from the east, west, south, or north; I must not remain unknown.
Thereupon, he had it consecrated with a mound four feet high.
What is now called the "Funtang" (Mound Hall) likely refers to a hall built at the site of the mound to house an image, which is the present-day Tiantai Pagoda Courtyard.

The *Biézhuan* records the Master’s final testament: “After my passing, at the location I have designated for my interment, pile stones around the body and plant pine trees to enclose it. Construct a stupa as a marker before it, so that those who see it may be inspired to resolve their minds toward the Way.”
Regarding the phrase "seeking the evidence" (*qiuzheng*): "seeking" means to search for;
"evidence" means verification.

Now, evidence applies to both the good and the evil. To show that being obstructed by attachments is an evil sign, one thereby knows that [the teachings] which have been abridged do not accord with the Master’s mind.
That there is no obstruction is a favorable omen; thus we know that the deletions and abridgments accord with the profound intent of the predecessors.
The *Shangshu* contains the "Auspicious Omens" (*xiuzheng*) and "Calamitous Omens" (*jiuzheng*), and the *Kongzhuan* states: "This records the evidence of good and evil deeds."
"Obstruction" refers to conditions such as illness.
"Two *xun*" means ten days constitute one *xun*. Regarding the phrase "the path to Buddhahood shall here conclude":

since the current *Lüshù* (Brief Commentary) has already reached nine fascicles and there are no longer any obstructions, we know that we have escaped the reproaches of the netherworld and will swiftly complete the path to Buddhahood; is this not the result of secret protection?
"寧" (níng) means "how could it be.
"Ouyōng" (mysterious and dark) refers collectively to the realm of Quiescent Light where the Great Master dwells.
Question:

Jingxi’s wondrous understanding and refined discernment—his pruning of the profuse and his selection of the essential—have enabled him to shoulder the Great Dharma; this truly falls upon my own person.
Why need one seek further verification before taking it as the standard?
Answer: There are two intentions.
First, to manifest that this is not a matter of casual practice, thereby encouraging future generations.
Second, it is to manifest that the work accords with the Master’s own intent, thereby precluding the slanders of others.
This is because, as the editorial revisions rested with me, those of shallow understanding at the time often criticized it; the ancients were just like those of today.
Wen Zhongzi said: "When Wang Zixu continued the Six Classics, some criticized him.
Xue Shou and Yao Yi informed me of this, and I sighed deeply, saying:
'If it were a wise man who criticized him, I would have adorned my sincerity to ask for forgiveness;'"
"It is not that the fool is at fault; how alone can I deal with him?
Third, "Tangbi" (Perhaps to Assist) and below clarify the author's humility and his stated intention.
The first two lines state his intention.
If this brief exposition can supplement the Great Master’s fundamental tenets, it will enable later students to understand them clearly and easily, free from the defects of prolixity and obscurity.
As the *Wenxuan* says: "The majestic war chariot shines brightly; the royal path gleams resplendently."
"Guang" refers to radiance or light.

His commentary states, "'Guangguang' means martial appearance," which is an error; it likely resulted from seeing the *Erya* say, "'Guangguang' and 'jiujiu' mean martiality," and thus providing this mistaken interpretation.

Regarding the phrase "posterity" (*hòukūn*): the *Gao of Zhong Hui* in the *Book of Documents* states, "He transmits ample benefits to posterity," and Kong Anguo’s *Commentary* explains, "He transmits the path of abundance and ease to demonstrate it to future generations."
"Jì zhū" (冀諸) below expresses self-humility.
"Jì" (冀) means to hope for.
Regarding "shù" (恕), the *Shēnglèi* states: "To measure others with one's own mind is called 'shù'."
II. The Commentary Text, in two parts:
First, the Title, in two parts: First, the Main Title.
The term "shu" (commentary) means to unravel and to resolve.
It unravels the text of the sutra and resolves the Buddha’s intent;
therefore, it is called a "shu. The *Wenxin diaolong* states: "Shu means to spread out."
The arrangement of the objects at the end summarizes the proximate meaning;
thus it is called the "Preface" (Sū).
Having distinguished between the subject and object, the explanation of the title of the sequence is already clear.
Question:
Why is it not titled "A Brief Commentary" (Lüshū)? Answer:
Since the title already states "The Sāman [Name] Abridged," there is no need for the character "abridged" (lue) within the title itself.

If the title were instead "Abridged Commentary" (Lüeshu), then beneath the title one would merely record the author's name; in that case, it would further be inappropriate to include characters such as "deleted" or "abridged."

For example, in Du Yu’s commentary on the *Chunqiu Zhuan*, since the title at the beginning reads "Collected Explanations of the Spring and Autumn Annals and its Tradition," only the two characters "Du Shi" (of the Du family) are written below.
When He Yan annotated the *Lunyu*, he simply titled it "Lunyu, Part One"; therefore, the subsequent text reads "Collected Explanations by He Yan."
Now, Jingxi’s intention in establishing the title is the same as He Yan’s.
Second, the brief explanation of the honorary title:
first, the explanation of the person; second, the brief explanation of the person.
"Tiantai" refers to the mountain where the Great Master resided.
Tao Hongjing’s *Zhen'gao* states: "The mountain is eighteen thousand *zhang* high and eight hundred *li* in circumference."
"The mountain has eight terraces, identical on all four sides; it lies within the divisions of the constellations Dou and Niu and corresponds above to the Tai Star, hence it is called Tiantai.
The two characters 'Zhizhe' (Wise One) are the honorary title of the Great Master."

Shenyong’s *Tiantai Ji* states: "When Emperor Yang was in the prince’s residence as the Prince of Jin, after the subjugation of Chen in the ninth year of the Kaihuang era, he requested the Great Master to confer upon him the Bodhisattva Precepts."
Once the King had received the precepts, he followed the *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra* in designating the Master as "Zhìzhě" (The Wise One).
As for the title "Dàshī" (Great Master), one who reviews what is old and knows what is new is called a "Master."
The *Fayan* says: "A teacher is the model and standard for humanity.
Xunzi said: "There are four arts of a teacher: one who is dignified and inspiring awe may be a teacher;
one who is mature and trustworthy may be a teacher; one whose recitations and expositions are not arrogant may be a teacher; and one who knows the subtle and can discourse upon it may be a teacher."
The term "Great" (Dà) is merely a designation used to express praise and magnificence.
As for "Exposition" (Shuō), the *Wenxin Diaolong* states: "To 'expound' (shuō) is to 'delight' (yuè)."
The trigram Dui represents the mouth and tongue; thus, speech is based on joy (*yue*).
Next is the abbreviated title:
"Śramaṇa. This is translated as "diligent cessation," meaning that one diligently practices various virtues and brings all evils to rest.
Those who pacify the evils within the realm of the world are the śramaṇas of the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings;
those who successively pacify the evils both within and without the realm of the world are the śramaṇas of the Distinct Teaching;
and those who universally pacify all evils, both internal and external, within a single mind are the śramaṇas of the Perfectly Integrated Teaching.
"Jingxi" refers to the person himself; his posthumous name was Zhànrán, and his secular surname was Qì.
His family had resided for generations at Jingxi in Jīnlíng, thus he was a native of Chángzhōu.
People honored his teachings and consequently took "Jingxi" as his title.
For over twenty years, he received the sutras from Zuoxi; following the Way as a retired scholar, he was joyfully followed by students.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era, he was finally registered in the monastic rolls at the age of thirty-seven.

He subsequently received the Vinaya precepts from Master Tányì of Huìkēi; he first resided in Qún and Jìnlíng in Wú, later traveled to Wútái, and finally settled at Tiāntái, in all of which locations he propagated and practiced the *Zhíguān*.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era and the beginning of the Dàlì era, successive imperial edicts summoned him, but he declined both times on the pretext of illness.

On the fifth day of the second month in the third year of Zhōngshèng of the Táng dynasty, he passed away at the Fólǒng Dào-chǎng; he was seventy-two years of age and thirty-four years of *dharmakṣaya* (monastic seniority).

During his ordinary days, he compiled and edited the teachings to clarify previous doubts and resolve subsequent obstructions; he followed and expounded upon everything transmitted within his own school, producing over one hundred fascicles that circulated widely throughout the world.

Therefore, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) of our Imperial Dynasty states: "Examining his work from the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era to the end of the Jiànzhōng era, he used his mind of self-realization to expound upon the Dharma never before heard."
Does not the Sūtra say, "To perform great Buddha-work in a brief moment"? Yet, it was Master [Daoxuan] who embodied this.
As for the term "abridged" (*lüe*), it means to prune away redundant words and preserve the essential meaning.
II. The Main Text, in two parts:
first, the opening of the chapters;
second, the detailed explanation, in five sections:
First, the sutra’s translation is incomplete, in two parts:
first, the explicit clarification of its incompleteness, in two parts:
first, distinguishing and indicating the Qin translation.
Regarding the "five translations": first, translated by the lay devotee Yan Fotiao of the Later Han dynasty, in one fascicle, titled the *Gǔ Wéimó jīng* (Old Vimalakīrti Sūtra).
Second, translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty, in two fascicles, titled the *Wéimójié shuō bùsī fǎmén jīng* (Sūtra on the Inconceivable Dharma Gate Spoken by Vimalakīrti).
3. Translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty, in one fascicle, titled *The Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate Expounded by Vimalakīrti*.
4. Translated by Zhu Shulan of the Western Jin Dynasty, in three fascicles, titled *The Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
Fifth, translated by Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty in three fascicles; this is the version currently being explained.
During the Tang dynasty, the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang translated it again in six fascicles, titled the *Buddhabhāṣita Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*.
In the present age, there are six translations; however, the scholar Zhi of the Sui dynasty saw only five.

Regarding the term "translation" (*yi*), the *Wangzhi* states: "The people of the five regions have languages that do not communicate with one another and desires that differ; [the ruler] must realize their intentions and facilitate their needs."
"In the east they are called *ji*; in the south, *xiang*; in the west, *didi*; and in the north, *yi*.
Zheng Xuan’s commentary states: "These are all colloquial names, applied according to their respective categories of activity."
The word *di* signifies "knowledge. Today, in the region of Ji (Ji Province), there is a term for a foreigner called *didì*; this is now a common term for Western languages.

As for the term *yì* (interpreter/translator), it is likely because during the Han dynasty affairs with the north were frequent, and the officials in charge of interpretation were also proficient in Western languages; thus, when Dharmakāla (Móténg) first arrived, he translated the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*.

Furthermore, regarding the term "transformation" (*fan*), the *Great Song Biographies of Eminent Monks* states: "It is like brocade or fine silk; both sides are beautiful, though the beauty differs according to which side faces left or right."
Regarding the phrase "Now, [I shall] explain Kumārajīva’s version": this is one among the five previous translations.
In Sanskrit he is called Kumārajīva, which is translated here as "Child-Longevity" (Tóngshòu).

Originally an Indian, he entered Chang’an only in the third year of the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin dynasty; by imperial decree, eight hundred śramaṇas were instructed to receive Kumārajīva’s teachings.

The ruler of Qin set aside the pride of his imperial station to honor the teachings of the Triple Gem, and at Cudamani Temple, together with three thousand monks, they took up the old translations to collate and finalize them, all of whom thoroughly penetrated their profound meanings.
From the fourth year to the eleventh year of the Hongshi era, Kumārajīva translated a total of ninety-eight scriptures comprising four hundred and twenty-one fascicles.
Sengrui, Sengzhao, Daochang, and others served as scribes; this particular scripture was translated in the eighth year of the Hongshi era.

Therefore, Sengzhao’s *Preface to the Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "The Celestial King of Daqin (the Great Qin) has frequently studied and contemplated this scripture, regarding it as the abode where the spirit dwells. Yet he regretted that the principles in the translations produced by Zhi [Qian] and Zhu [Fonian] were obstructed by the phrasing, and he constantly feared that the profound essence would be lost through the errors of the translators."

In the eighth year of the Hongshi era, he commanded the Great General, Duke of Changshan, and the Right General, Marquis of Ancheng, together with twelve hundred śramaṇas of the school of righteousness, to invite Dharma Master Kumārajīva at the Great Monastery in Chang’an to retranslate the authentic text.
2. "Next, 'Examining the Sūtra' (Xun Jing) and below" provides a comparative analysis of the extensive and abbreviated versions in two parts:
first, it clarifies that the Sanskrit original is still extensive, in two sub-sections:
first, a general heading that introduces the inquiry;
Second, from "As [stated] in the *Life*" (*Rujing*) onwards, the text is cited to provide the correct demonstration.

The Great Master searched through five passages and their meanings, discovering that the Indian Sanskrit manuscripts still contained many more sections: first, the "Chapter on Disciples" (*Dizi pin*); second, the "Chapter on Bodhisattvas" (*Pusa pin*); third, the "Chapter on Inquiring after Illness" (*Wenji pin*); fourth, the "Chapter on the Gate of Non-duality" (*Buermen pin*); and fifth, the two chapters on "Bodhisattva Practice" (*Pusaxing*) and "Akṣobhya Buddha" (*Achufo*).
These five phrases do not fully exhaust the meaning; their sequence is indicated within the text.

As for the phrase "these five hundred," this refers to the point in the *Śrāvaka-varga* where, after the ten individuals have been named, the narrator records that these five hundred great disciples each recounted their own original causes and conditions.

Regarding the phrase "up to eight thousand," this refers to the section on the Bodhisattvas where, after the four individuals have been summoned, the narrator describes how each of these bodhisattvas spoke to the Buddha concerning their own past causes and conditions.
Question:
At the end of the "Bodhisattva Chapter," it merely says "all bodhisattvas"; how can it be said that there are eight thousand? Answer:

At the beginning of the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter, the sutra states: "Immediately, eight thousand bodhisattvas and five hundred śrāvakas all desired to follow along. From this, we know that it was these eight thousand people who were summoned within the "Bodhisattva" chapter.

Below the phrase "unable to [endure]," five hundred and eight thousand [monks] all together declined their inability; it is certain that each of these phrases exists in its own form in the Sanskrit original.
Below the phrase "Furthermore, the text," is the "Chapter on Inquiring after Illness" (*Vyākarana-parivarta*).
"Boundless earnestness" refers to Mañjuśrī’s recounting of the Buddha’s intent.
The sutra states: "The World-Honored One sends boundless greetings with earnest concern.
The section beginning with "In addition to the eight" refers to the "Chapter on the Gate of Non-duality."
Eight thousand bodhisattvas followed him into the room and spoke of what they had realized; they should have fully recounted it all, yet the scriptural text mentions only thirty-two individuals.

Regarding the phrase "these various discourses," if one were to record in full the immeasurable questions of Mañjuśrī and exhaustively describe the dharma-gates of non-duality of all eight thousand bodhisattvas, how could this occupy no more than half a fascicle?
The phrase "down to" (*yuánzhì*) refers to the two chapters, "Bodhisattva Practice" (*Púsàxíng*) and "Akṣobhya Buddha" (*Āchùfó*).
*Yuán* means "to say"; it is merely a particle.

Regarding "Going to the Āmra Garden," this refers to Vimalakīrti personally escorting the great assembly back to the Āmra Garden, where he once again addressed the Buddha to clarify the meaning of the Buddha-lands.
The *Shangshu* says, "He responded to the auspicious mandate of the Son of Heaven," and Kong Anguo’s *Commentary* states, "'Responded' means 'replied.
He replied upon receiving the beautiful mandate and extolled it.
Regarding the phrase "an exchange of lofty discourse": "exchange" (wǎngfù) means that one side asks (wèn) and the other responds (dá).
The expression "how could it be contained in merely a few sheets of paper? implies that the text of these two chapters is even more extensive.
Second, to show that this land should be treated briefly:
"Zhendan" (China) may also be rendered as Zhendan, Zhendan, or Zhinan; all are transcriptions of the Sanskrit sound *Cīna*.
If one follows the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra to translate this into the land of Han, furthermore, there are two pronunciations for it in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*:
the first is *Cīna*, which means "land of arts and letters. This praises our region as a land of refined dress and cultural refinement.
The second is called "Yunzhi" (Cloud-Point), which here is translated as "Frontier Barbarian"; this is a derogatory term used to disparage this region as not being the Central Kingdom (*madhyadeśa*).
The *Record of the Western Regions* translates Mahācīna as the "Great Han Kingdom."

II. Re-examination based on the title, in two parts:

First, the intent of the question: Since the title of the *Avataṃsaka* lacks the designation "Inconceivable" (*acintya*), whereas the title of the present sutra clearly contains that name, why do you conversely claim that the "Inconceivable Sutra" referred to in the *Śāstra* is not this present sutra?
2. The Response, in two parts:
First, an analogical counter-interrogation.
Regarding the phrase "there is no other designation," what prevents the *Avataṃsaka* from having another name, namely "Inconceivable"?
2. From "However, [it is] subtle" onwards, the treatise is cited to demonstrate that [the previous view] is incorrect.

Regarding the phrase "This is precisely the matter explained in the *Avataṃsaka*": the fortieth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva clarifies that the laywoman Huishè (Śreṣṭhī) explained to Sudhana the number of sentient beings to be delivered; this is identical to what is cited in the *Śāstra* from the *Acintya-sūtra* concerning Akṣobhya and others. Therefore, it is known that the "Inconceivable Sūtra" mentioned in the treatise must certainly be the *Avataṃsaka*.
Regarding the phrase "If one cites... and below: whenever the treatise cites this present sutra, it explicitly states that it is the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
This is because people, seeing that this sutra has the single name *Acintyavimokṣa*, assume it must be the *Acintya-sūtra* cited in the *Śāstra*.
Since what has been grasped is incorrect, this [section] provides a detailed refutation.
Second, a brief division of the text, in two parts:
first, the opening of the chapters.
2. Sequential Explanation, in two parts:
first, the explanation provided by various masters.
"Shisheng" refers to Kumārajīva and Daosheng.
The phrase "and Zhaor" refers to Sengzhao’s commentary on the sutra, which explains the single term "inconceivable liberation.
"Kaishan" is the name of a monastery; it refers to Dharma Master Zhizang.
Regarding the "Three Verifications": this refers to [Huiyuan] carrying the great assembly in his hands back to the monastery garden to verify the matter before the Buddha.

As for the passage beginning with "If one decorates," it refers to Sengmin of Sisi Temple, Fayun of Guangzhai Temple, and Zhizang of Kaishan Temple, all of whom were contemporaries during the Liang dynasty; they were collectively known as the Three Great Dharma Masters.
"The Three Treatises" refers to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the *Śataśāstra*, and the *Dvādaśamukhaśāstra*; in ancient times, these three treatises were widely propagated.
"The Northern Land Masters" refers to the masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha* at Hébì.
"Much contention and strife" means that [the teachings] were extended, advanced, and became disordered.

First, refuting errors according to the ancients;
second, from "Now I seek" onwards, revealing what is correct based on the present [text].
Regarding the phrase "collateral sutras and opening of sections," Jingxi said:
This is because their intentions and inclinations differ from those of the two masters.
They differ from other Chan masters by relying on the auxiliary scriptures; they differ from other Dharma masters by not being dogmatic.

As for the statement, "The exposition is most complete," it refers to the five periods of teaching being distinct and the skillful accommodations for various capacities being differentiated; thus, they are said to have "diverse origins."
The source is the initial overflow of water; this serves as a metaphor for the beginning of an opportune connection (*kai-ki*).
Although the five periods [of the Buddha's teaching] are not uniform, there is no fault of missing the opportune moment; thus, one is able to achieve a good beginning and a successful conclusion.
It possesses three meanings:

since the introduction (*nidāna*) fundamentally introduces the main body (*samyak*), and the dissemination (*parīndanā*) extends through the main body, these three must not be deficient; therefore, it is said to be "complete.
Second, from "Now, regarding... below, the opening of the chapters has two parts:
Below "The First Correctness," the meaning is presented according to the chapters, in three parts:
first, the formal opening of the sutra, which has two sub-sections;
first, a general presentation of the three sections found in all sutras.

In ancient times, there were no chapter divisions when directly explaining the scriptural texts; the practice of dividing the sutra into three sections began with Dao’an, and subsequent generations followed this, thereby establishing it as a standard rule.

From the words "If one wishes" onwards, three scriptures are cited which speak of "relying upon signs"; these all refer to obtaining the opportunity to preach the Dharma by means of the manifestation of auspicious omens.
Regarding "light of variegated colors": light symbolizes the illumination and realization of *prajñā*, while variegation symbolizes the distinctions among the various practices (*saṃskāra*).
Guided by wisdom, all practices converge in the single suchness (*tathatā*), just as light does nothing but illuminate.
Because practice follows wisdom, as the various practices are distinct, so too is wisdom; it is like light mixed with various colors.
Jingxi said: "Prajñā is illumination;

therefore, light symbolizes it. This is why that sutra repeatedly emits light, just as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, where the emission of light symbolizes the middle [truth]; thus, all three sections of the *Lotus Sūtra* are 'middle'."
As in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, permanence is indicated by the emission of light; thus, these three are likewise all permanent.
Therefore, we know that in this present sūtra, the manifestation of the land indicates the land itself, and all three are collectively the Buddha-land.
To deeply comprehend this principle, the various teachings become brilliantly clear.
If this is so, why does the *Lotus Sūtra* not take the "Middle" as its primary tenet? Answer:
Since the principle of grasping [the truth] is identical to the ultimate limit (bhūtakoṭi) and there is nothing that is not the One Vehicle, it is called the "Introduction" (nidāna).
Furthermore, this introduction is twofold:
the manifestation of auspicious omens and the formal narration.

If one discusses the causes and conditions, they exist solely in the manifestation of omens; the narrative merely recounts those previously manifested omens as well as the two types of causes—proximate and remote.
Furthermore, there are some sūtras that lack such a narrative.
Therefore, the general exposition of the meaning of the "Preface" (xu) here concerns solely the manifestation of auspicious omens (*nimitta*).

Regarding the phrase "capable of hearing the Sage’s intent," Jingxi says: "Thus we know that because the omens were manifested, the conditions for the responsive capacity (*mūla*) of sentient beings were moved; there is indeed a profound reason for the name 'Initiation' (*faqi*)."

Furthermore, just as the disparagement of the minor and the rebuke of the major occurred in the past, although these were not auspicious signs, they nevertheless foreshadowed the present sutra; their favorable omens appeared in advance to assist in the accomplishment of the present matter.
Since their meaning supports the correct [teaching], it is appropriate that they be presented first.
Regarding "unobstructed and unhindered," Jingxi says: "Hindrance" refers to internal dharmas that block, while "obstruction" refers to external objects that shield;

yet from the flow [of the teaching] down to the age of the Semblance Dharma, there is none who is not moistened by it. Thus, there is no obstruction or hindrance—this is entirely the power of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the terms "Right Dharma" (*saddharma*) and "Semblance Dharma" (*pratirūpaka-dharma*): after the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, the Dharma undergoes three periods.
In the case of Śākyamuni, the Right Dharma and the Semblance Dharma each last for one thousand years, while the Final Dharma (*antardharma*) lasts for ten thousand years.
When the four—principle, teaching, practice, and fruit—are all fully complete, it is called the True Dharma (*saddharma*), as when the Buddha was still in the world.
Although the first three exist, if the realization of the fruit is entirely absent, it is called the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*).
"Image" (*xiàng*) means "resemblance," for it resembles the True Dharma.
Since practitioners have become few and the principles and teachings remain only as vestiges, while the Dharma has already declined to its final stage, it is called the "Final Dharma" (*mofa*).
Regarding the term "this moisture" (*sīzé*): "moisture" (*zé*) means "to nourish."
Second, from "Now, opening" (*jin kai*) onwards, there is a separate section analyzing the current text, which has two parts:
first, the primary division into three sections;
second, from "Question" (*wen*) onwards, the explanation of difficulties based on terminology.

The intent of the question is that since it was previously stated that all eleven chapters clarify the causes and effects of the Buddha-land as the primary teaching, [the questioner asks for clarification].
The intent of the answer is that a text only becomes a sūtra once it has been authenticated by the Buddha’s seal of approval.
Although the title refers to Vimalakīrti, the meaning ultimately returns to the Buddha-land as the primary teaching; thus, it perfectly captures the essential purport of the sutra.
Within the response, there are three parts: the principle (dharma), the analogy, and the application.
Regarding the term "propagating government" (*bùzhèng*), Huang Kan stated that "government" (*zhèng*) refers to laws and regulations.
Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Rites of Zhou* (*Zhōu Lǐ*) states that "government is that which rectifies what is not correct."

Regarding the phrase "and the minister receives the reward," the *Shangshu* states: "For those who are diligent in virtue, confer office upon them; for those who are diligent in merit, confer rewards upon them.
The commentary notes: "'Diligent' (mào) means 'to exert oneself' (miǎn)."
"Those who strive for virtue are encouraged by means of office;
those who strive for merit are encouraged by means of reward.
Regarding the statement, "Only when one reaches purity and impartiality does one attain correctness," Jingxi said:
The Dharma can be certified as the True Sūtra, but how could a person be certified as a Master of Transformation?
Regarding the "second point, observing the mind": if one does not observe one's own mind, it is like a poor person counting another's treasures.

The liberation of all Buddhas is sought within the activities of the mind; therefore, by adhering to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one accomplishes sublime contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

In this text, for the time being, the three divisions are elucidated according to the sequential Threefold Contemplation (*san-ti san-kuān*); although the explanation follows a sequence, its underlying intent returns to the single mind.
Regarding the phrase "the mind and mind are quiescent," Jingxi says:
"One should follow the literal meaning as it appears in the text for the sake of its circulation; the same applies to the gate of contemplation, and thus this interpretation is made."
3. Differing from other masters, there are six points.
First, differing from Master Shi and the Chan Master:
regarding the phrase "knowing the beginning and end of the text," Jingxi says this refers to the meaning at the beginning and end of each chapter, as divided in the text.

Within the Main Body, there are the sections on outside the room, inside the room, and leaving the room. Leaving the room is further divided into the categories of emptiness, conventionality, and the Middle Way.
2. Differing from Master Zhao.

Regarding the statement "the meaning is not so": in the "Dharma-Offering" chapter, Śakra praises the propagation of the sutra, and the Buddha clarifies that the offering of the Dharma is supreme; this concerns the circulation [of the teaching], not the primary exposition itself.
3. Different Flavors: Two parts.
First, the question.
Second, the answer, which has three parts:
First, a general refutation.
Second, from "What is it? onwards, the formal refutation.
Regarding the term "Dao-wang" (King of the Way), "wang" is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

Regarding "attaining great and small benefits": when the pure land was manifested, five hundred attained patience (*kṣānti*) and eighty thousand resolved their minds on enlightenment; this is attaining great benefit.

When the land became defiled again, gods and humans attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣurviśuddhi*), and bhikṣus reached the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) with liberated minds; this is attaining small benefit.
Since the purpose of responding to the occasion is to discern the Way for the benefit of others, how can such [teachings] be disparaged as not being the correct doctrine?
Therefore, it is said: "How could one disparage this as merely an introduction?"

"Furthermore, 'Vimalakīrti’s purity reaches the Buddha's teaching'" means that if it were not for the seal of the Buddha, it could not be called a sūtra; thus we know that Vimalakīrti’s purity assists the Buddha’s transformation of beings from the side.
Third, "How could it be... and below concludes with a reprimand.
Fourth, it differs from the Kaishan school.

That school employs the names of the three divisions—Introduction, Proper Exposition, and Dissemination—and further adds the "Establishment of Proof" to constitute four divisions; therefore, it is not universally applicable.
If that were so, then Zhiyi’s division of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* into five sections would also be incorrect.
However, the purpose of dividing a sūtra into sections is to clarify its underlying principles; since the meaning of this sūtra is already clear within three divisions, what need is there for four?

The purport of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is not revealed unless the five [aspects] are present; how much less could it establish separate names and characteristics as Kai-shan did by adding the name "three parts" to make four?
As it says: "First, the invitation to the assembly of *nirvāṇa*, up to the fifth, the application of *nirvāṇa* through breaking and gathering," and so forth.
Fifth, the various adornments of the masters, in two parts:
first, the question.
2. The Response, in two parts:
first, a judgment that the introductory section is incorrect;
second, from "Furthermore, as for its function" onwards, a judgment that the section on circulation is incorrect.
"Returning to the causes and effects regarding Vimalakīrti" refers to the "Akṣobhya Chapter," which restates the fundamental doctrine concerning the causes and effects of the Buddha-land.

Regarding "summarizing the beginning and end of the sutra": the Buddha-land is the beginning and Akṣobhya is the end; both discuss the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment as the retribution of support).
If the underlying intent is such as this, how can it be considered a means for circulation?
Regarding the phrase "passing through the inner chamber": when the Land of Wondrous Joy was manifested in the "Akṣobhya Chapter," fourteen nayutas of people resolved their minds on Bodhi;
however, in the "Inconceivable Chapter" within the inner chamber, when Kāśyapa uttered his lamentation, only thirty-two thousand devaputras resolved their minds on Bodhi.
At the end of the "Inquiry into Illness" chapter (*Vyākarana-parivarta*), there are only eight thousand [stanzas].
Sixth, regarding the Mahayana masters of the Northern Regions:
