He follows along with what is beautiful and rectifies or rescues what is evil; therefore, it is said, "showing him with clarity and penetration."
Thereafter, within this True Dharma, he points out and demonstrates the principle of arising and ceasing, as well as non-arising, in accordance with the four types of spiritual faculties.
Fifteen: Manifesting as a Prince.

Regarding "being clear-sighted and proficient in filial piety," the *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "One draws upon the service rendered to one's father to serve one's mother, and the love is the same.
One draws upon the service rendered to one's father to serve one's ruler, and the reverence is the same."
Vimalakīrti is able to speak of filial piety and reverence; therefore, he is held in high esteem.
Sixteenth, he manifests himself as an inner court official.

Regarding the term "palace women" (*gung-nu*): if one follows the conventions of this region, it is as stated in the *Rites of Zhou*: "The Queen of the Son of Heaven establishes the six palaces, the three ladies (*fu-ren*), the nine concubines (*pin*), the twenty-seven senior wives (*shi-fu*), and the eighty-one attendants (*yu-qi*)."
Zheng’s commentary states: "The former refers to one palace, and the latter refers to five palaces.

As for the five, they are: one palace for the Queen; one palace for the three Consorts; one palace for the nine Ladies-in-Waiting; one palace for the twenty-seven Senior Wives; and one palace for the eighty-one Attendant Women."
Later, when she was formally installed in the inner palace, her status was equal to that of the Heavenly King (the Emperor).

The First Lady sat in council to discuss the rites of women, while the Nine Consorts took charge of teaching the four virtues. The Worldly Ladies oversaw the knowledge of mourning rituals, sacrifices, and state guests, and the Palace Attendants attended to the King’s private chambers.

According to the Han system, there were fourteen ranks in the inner palace: these were the Zhaoyi (Court Lady of Bright Splendor), Jieyu (Lady of Grace), Ying’uo (Lady of Elegant Form), Ronghua (Lady of Refinement), Meiren (Beauty), Bazi (Eighth-Rank Lady), Chongyi (Lady of Full Robes), Qizizi (Seventh-Rank Lady), Liangren (Virtuous Woman), Changshi (Senior Messenger), Shaoshi (Junior Messenger), Wuguan (Five-Office Lady), Shunchang (Lady of Accordance), and Wucheng (Lady of Purity). These constitute the fourteen ranks.
Ban Gu’s *Xi du fu* states: "The titles of the ladies in the inner palace number fourteen.
This refers precisely to this.
Regarding the phrase "giving rise to internal depraved thoughts," Zhaolun says: "Because women are by nature prone to seductive charms and depraved adornments, they are instructed in uprightness."
The phrase "the fourfold eightfold path" refers to the eightfold noble path within the four teachings.
Seventeenth, he manifests among the common people.
"Common" (shu) means the multitude; it refers to the masses of people throughout the world.
18. Manifesting as Being in the Brahma Heavens.

Regarding the "eighteen Brahma heavens": the first, second, and third dhyānas each have three heavens, while the fourth dhyāna has nine; all are free from the defilement of desire and are thus collectively termed "Brahma."
Regarding the phrase "instructing with supreme wisdom," Jingxi says:

For instance, among the branches of dhyāna-contemplation, some are wisdom but not supreme; even Brahmā once attained them, yet they are not regarded as venerable. Therefore, [the Buddha] demonstrates the four kinds of supramundane supreme wisdom, pure dhyāna-contemplations, and so forth, as well as the stainless dhyāna. These are exceptionally superior, clearly manifesting the fundamental practice while remaining free from attachment.
Nineteen: Manifesting as Śakra.
Regarding the "Fifteen Contemplation Gates," one must await further investigation and exposition.
As for the statement, "In the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), everything from the *Vajra* [Samādhi] downward is impermanent," Jingxi says:
This is what others have calculated; we shall now judge it and assign it to the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna).
Furthermore, the Brahma King maintains his permanence even beyond that of Śakra, and claims to be the father and mother of all sentient beings.

Therefore, when it is said that the Brahmās today do not take impermanence as their antidote, it is because those Brahmās have already attained the profound fundamental dhyānas; they merely use superior wisdom to supplant their outflows (*āsrava*).

As for the Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and others, they all generally maintain the notion of permanence; here too, setting aside their general state, they are described according to their specific individualities, and this is precisely why [the distinction is made].
Furthermore, because he also wishes to demonstrate that the various gateways of the teaching differ from one another so that they may be universally recognized, he speaks of each separately.
Twenty: To show that [the Buddha] resides among the Four Heavenly Kings.

Regarding the phrase "each presiding over two classes of spirits and deities": the east presides over the gandharvas and piśācas; the south presides over the kumbhāṇḍas and preta; the west presides over the venomous nāgas and pūtanas; and the north presides over the yakṣas and rākṣasas.

Below the phrase "the preceding one by one," there is a general indication that the aforementioned thirty-five matters are all intended to support the realization of the Buddha-land; those who expound this teaching should understand their fundamental principle.
III. Conclusion. II.
Eight chapters and a half explaining the skillful means for the benefit of sound, in two parts:
first, the section stating the intent and dividing the structure, in two parts: [1] ... [2] ... (as per the original structure).
First, the statement of intent, in two parts:
first, the general statement.
Regarding the phrase "removing the defilements of material offenses," Jingxi says:
The designation "defilement of transgression" (pāpa-mala) must be understood across all four teachings.

Because it arises from the convergence of two conditions, within each section of these teaching gates, the extensive and the concise reflect one another; one should explain them by following their respective thematic tendencies. Where an explanation ought to be extensive, one must not allow the brevity of the phrasing to cause the meaning to become muddled; thus, when seeing a general summary, one should expand upon it through specific details, or when encountering specific texts, one should subsume them under a general principle.

Therefore, the substance of delusion is non-dual and wisdom is not established by anything else; from the one, all are opened, and all are made to return to the one. When seen in union, there is no deficiency; when separated at the source, there is nothing divided. This is true for the body and the land, as well as for delusion and wisdom—all are thus.
Therefore, the elimination of views and the removal of defilements constitute the causes for the four lands; how could it be merely a matter of the "realm within" (dharmadhātu)?
Second, the detailed exposition of the intent has three parts:
first, the listing of the chapters.
Regarding the title "The Chapter on Initiating the Inquiry into Illness," Jingxi said: "If one asks why,
among the six chapters concerning the interior [of the palace], only this one is titled 'Initiating the Inquiry into Illness,' the answer is as follows:"
The six grades of delusions regarding internal phenomena all arise from illness; however, by specifically designating "inquiring after illness," the other five are naturally subsumed.
Second, from "The Initial Meaning" onwards, is the formal explanation.
Regarding the phrase, "Entrust these words to using 'reproach' as a means for exhortation," Jingxi says:

For instance, when it is said, "This body is impermanent," one uses the illness of one's own body to reproach the opponent's attachment to permanence; by using reproach as an exhortation to contemplate the Dharma-body, a single act of reproach thus contains the meaning of both exhortation and admonition. How much more so when, following the admonition, one immediately exhorts the contemplation!

It should be stated as "entering the inconceivable liberation"; the character "not" (bu) is omitted in the text. This means that, in the distant sense, it serves as the introductory lead for entering the inconceivable, and in the proximate sense, it serves as the cause for the two lands.
Regarding the phrase "Birth, dwelling together, and having a remainder," etc., Jingxi says:

Because one views both the exhaustion and non-exhaustion of severed conditioned phenomena as objects of vision, this constitutes a remote cause for realizing liberation through vision, while losing the immediate practice of a Mahāsattva.
Regarding the phrase "How could I dare to venture to recount it," Jingxi said:
"Feeling shame for the past and remorse for the present, my mind is filled with trepidation; who would not feel constrained to refrain from venturing to recount their humble thoughts?"

Having been commanded to urge [the Emperor] to ascend the throne, I feared that doing so would once again invite base shame; though I have schemed to comply with the situation, it has already become a matter of yielding my principles. To recount my faults before the Buddha is far superior to being repeatedly ridiculed by the common world; therefore, I shall speak based on the fundamental truth while simultaneously proclaiming the transformative Way. In this way, both guest and host, as well as teacher and disciple, will all derive benefit from the provisional and the ultimate.

"Delighting in the small and clinging to the small" means that delighting in the small is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Hīnayāna, while clinging to the small refers to those who, within the Hīnayāna, perceive the existence of a fruit.

"Aspiring to the Mahāyāna" means that upon knowing there is a Mahāyāna, one gives rise to a vision of it and develops reverence; at that time, one will certainly be able to generate the Great Mind (*mahācitta*).

Regarding the phrase "attaining [this] constitutes a most excellent condition": if there were no refutation and censure, one would be incapable of being refined and purified; moreover, since the two flavors serve as the cause for perceiving the *amṛta* (clarified butter), those who receive the prediction and relinquish their lives will inevitably bring forth the fruit of retribution.
Regarding the phrase "Universally causing the three teachings," Jingxi says:
"Although there are three teachings, the primary intent is to use the Perfect [Teaching] to critique the various bodhisattvas.

Since the bodhisattvas do not abide in the great principle and their views on seeing are the same as those of the Śrāvakas, those of the Tripitaka and Shared [teachings] then use the Distinct [Teaching] to refute their attachments."

Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): within the Vaipulya [teachings], those of sharp faculties enter into the ultimate reality while those of dull faculties have not yet done so; thus we know that herein the three terms are applied universally.
Alternatively, they merely enter into the general and the particular, and it is only at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that all are seen to return to the realization of the truth.
However, according to the general tenor of the sutras, one must enter into reality, because the true nature is taken as the essence and the four lands are taken as the central theme.
Herein, we shall speak from the perspective of contrasting them with the ultimate.
3. From "This" onwards, the conclusion and demonstration are provided.
Regarding "these four meanings," Jingxi says:
"They are exactly as listed and explained in the preceding text."
Furthermore, summarizing the four preceding intentions, there are another four specific points:
first, Mañjuśrī attains his life; second, Mañjuśrī discusses the Way; third, the śrāvakas feel self-contempt; and fourth, the bodhisattvas advance in their practice.
Thus we know that the former two serve to establish the latter two.
Furthermore, the latter two possess both distant and proximate meanings; these distant and proximate meanings are again twofold:
first, the general, and second, the particular.
What is called "penetration" (tong) refers to the fact that both the distant and the near each have their own dimensions of distance and proximity.
Regarding the two types of śrāvakas: the distant refers to those who achieve the ultimate, while the near refers to those who enter the stage of "ripened butter" (pakva-ghṛta).
Regarding the two types of bodhisattvas: the dull-witted are the same as the two vehicles in that they perceive the existence of a vehicle, whereas the sharp-witted realize it immediately.
Regarding the distinction mentioned: the benefit for *śrāvakas* is remote, while the benefit for *bodhisattvas* is immediate.
Since this commentary follows the specific [distinction], the *śrāvakas* feel self-disparagement, whereas the *bodhisattvas* advance in their practice.
Regarding the phrase "Now, 'clarifying'... and below, the section is divided into two parts:
first, the general division. Jingxi says:
Regarding the statement that "the *Yì* [Sūtra] has four sections and two parts," the four are as listed above.

As for the "two parts," they are as found in the current text: subduing (*zhé-fú*) and gathering (*shè-shòu*), which may also be treated as two, namely, gathering within the room and subduing outside the room.

Within the context of subduing (*nigraha*), there is both the present and the past: the "present" refers to the lay followers who inquired after his illness, while the "past" refers to the monastic community that was rebuked.
Within the context of gathering (*saṃgraha*), there are likewise two meanings: the producer and the produced; the "producer" refers to the empty room, and the "produced" refers to the six chapters.
Furthermore, this may also be divided into the perspectives of self and other: the former conveys the Buddha’s intent, while the latter expresses one’s own sentiments.

Specifically, from the passage beginning with "The householder is ill" onwards, the following concerns matters outside [the chamber]. Since thousands of people had already gone to inquire after his illness, at that time he had not yet manifested inconceivable deeds for the sake of the elders and kings; therefore, we see instances where there were those who came to inquire after his illness.
Although the sick person is actually inside the room, that which they are affected by—the mechanical forms—is all external; thus it is said to be "outside the room.
Speaking from the perspective of what is affected, it is further described as being "outside the room."

Furthermore, regarding "subduing and gathering" (*śāsanasaṃgraha*) and so forth, one may understand them by reflecting upon the meaning of the three skillful means (*upāya*) from the *Śrīgarbha-sūtra* (瓔珞經).

As for "subduing within which gathering is fully contained," and so on: subduing is like analytical contemplation (*vibhāga-vipaśyanā*), while gathering is like contemplation of the essence (*svabhāva-vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, "breaking" (analyzing) is like the contemplation of the body, while "gathering" (synthesizing) is like the exhortation to seek [the Dharma].
Moreover, within gathering, "breaking" refers to subduing, while "gathering" refers to comforting and seeing what is seen.
Furthermore, general breaking encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate, while specific breaking encompasses the perfect; additionally, provisional breaking is encompassed by the real.
"Up to 'neither provisional nor real,'" the subsequent passages show the categories of seeing and being seen; these can be understood through inference.
Second, "Now, as for... and below, there is a separate division into two parts:
first, the actual classification.
Regarding the phrase "this is the subduing of the collection of conditions within one's own substance," Jingxi says:
[The questioner asks: Previously, you already refuted the two types of collections established by the ancients; why do you now further establish a "collection of one's own substance"?

Answer: This is done both to refute the specific designation established by the masters of those treatises and because we now establish only a single unconditioned aggregate; therefore, it is appropriate to designate it as such.
Furthermore, in this present text, we first provisionally rely on their own established name for its essential nature in order to implicitly supersede it.
Second, the critical analysis (*liaojian*), in two parts:
regarding the first section, Jingxi states:

"From the question-and-answer section below, there is a re-elucidation of its faults; the subsequent discernment of the slight differences in how the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna receive their names constitutes the formal explanation."
However, one must grasp the essential meaning of the correct interpretation, while also intending to refute [erroneous] views.

The masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explain internal and external *dharmas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in conjunction with ignorance; here, it is stated that both the followers of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas alike possess internal and external unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) accumulations of conditions.

Once it has been distinguished, it is immediately perceived as seeing; whereas the two vehicles must establish their names based on attachment to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the Bodhisattva is without such attachment and contemplates only the self-nature and the *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, it receives a distinct name and is called the *dharmadhātu*.

The Dharma-realm is not a condition (*pratyaya*), for conditions merge with the essence of that Dharma-realm; it is spoken of as such from the perspective of what is obstructed, hence it is said that "the self-essence of the Dharma-realm arises through the collection of conditions.

For this reason, one must set aside the "dust-sands" [of afflictions] established from ignorance; since these dust-sand delusions do not collectively draw forth birth within or outside the realms, they are temporarily set aside and not established from them.
Therefore, the text states: "The names differ, but the substance is the same.
Consequently, it is illustrated that the learner (śaikṣa) and the ordinary person (pṛthagjana) alike possess the afflictions of volition within the three realms.
This passage consists of two parts:
First, the question;
second, the answer, which has two parts:
first, the direct answer.
2. "As with ordinary people," and so forth, introduces an illustrative example.
Regarding the two instances, Jingxi says:
As for the question concerning "study" and so on, this question arises from the preceding answer.
If both the True [Nature] and the Middle [Way] can be termed "principle" (*li*),
and since the delusions attached to the Middle are termed "intrinsic" (*svabhāva*), would the delusions based on the True [Nature] also be termed "intrinsic delusions"?
Since the previous answer employed the terminology of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra* masters, I shall now follow that very same terminology to pose this further challenge.
The meaning of the response is as follows: since the two truths are distinct, their essential meanings differ.

Consequently, the [defiled] realm within the obstructions is entirely not the same essence [as the truth]; it cannot be given a name identical to that established for the [unobstructed] truth. Furthermore, since the essences of the two delusions are fundamentally different—being eternally separate as coarse and subtle—and the two truths are inherently separated, why should they be forcibly made the same?

Therefore, we know that the "self-nature" (svabhāva) manifests as the "partial truth" (pradeśasatya) when contrasted with the "middle"; it is neither a self nor a nature in itself, but merely established in opposition to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). Since it cannot be separately established apart from this contrast, the principle of refuting it based on what precedes remains valid.

Regarding the phrase "How is it known to be so?": "So" (ran) means "thus" (ru ci), serving as a reference to what precedes; it asks, "By what means can one know that Vimalakīrti’s lying ill manifests these two kinds of conditions?"

The meaning of the answer is as follows: His unconditional great compassion pervades the ten realms, and there is no one among those called "sentient beings" whom it does not encompass; therefore, we know that his manifesting illness was intended to lead the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones to attain freedom from illness.
2. The reason for conforming to the Lesser Vehicle.

The intent of the question is this: Since Vimalakīrti manifests as a layman but is in fact a bodhisattva, and since he has already attained mastery over the two types of illness, why must he conform to the Lesser Vehicle?
The meaning of the response is that the universal manifestation [of the Buddha]—how could it obstruct the Two Vehicles?

From the words "Furthermore" onwards, it refers specifically to manifesting for Bodhisattvas of the four teachings; however, the Shared Teaching already subsumes the Two Vehicles because what they realize is the same.

Regarding the "ten perceptions" (*shi xiang*), Jingxi said:
This is fully detailed in the *Dharmadhātusthāna* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).
Regarding the phrase "the first three," these are impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
Regarding the "middle four," these are the impurity of food, the world as being unworthy of delight, and the impurity of death.
The latter three are abandonment (*prahāṇa*), detachment (*virāga*), and exhaustion (*kṣaya*).

Regarding the phrase "now, concerning the exhortation to seek" and so forth: if one enters the latter three, one immediately enters the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); therefore, they are not mentioned here.
Regarding the phrase "in terms of two kinds of foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*): Question:
Why is it not explained in terms of the foundation of mindfulness as objects (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*)? Answer:

The ten similes are: first, an illusion; second, a mirage; third, the moon reflected in water; fourth, empty space; fifth, an echo; sixth, a city of the gandharvas; seventh, a dream; eighth, a shadow; ninth, a reflection; and tenth, a magical creation.

If even the four great elements are merely provisional, how much more so should sentient beings be understood to be.
2. From "Now, to clarify" below, the present explanation is set forth in two parts:
first, the refutation by examining the four subtle elements (*paramāṇu*).
Regarding the phrase "composed of the four internal subtle elements," Jingxi says:
This is explained here merely in accordance with external doctrines; indeed, such a doctrine exists among the twenty-five *tattvas*.

Thus, when they say that within the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) there is a slight increase or decrease [in their constituent atoms], the intended meaning is that those whose power is weak must be composed of many atoms, whereas those whose power is great are composed of few atoms.

Therefore, among the four great elements, the power of wind is the greatest; it alone constitutes a subtle entity, whereas water lacks the subtle element of fragrance and fire lacks the subtle elements of both fragrance and taste. At first glance, it may indeed appear to be so.
However, within the Buddha-dharma, not even a single atom can independently constitute a phenomenon; rather, all material entities are composed of four types of atoms.
Now, in order to refute their [erroneous] calculations, we follow their own reckoning; thus, it is said below that "fire is composed of two types of atoms," and so forth.

Regarding the passage "If internally," since the four great elements have no master, how could the three matters not be likewise? For among these three matters, vitality is the element of wind, warmth is the element of fire, and consciousness is the element of consciousness within the six great elements.

The phrase "If water reaches you, it is likewise [sentient]" raises the analogy of water to challenge the existence of a conscious deity.

The passage beginning with "If you say that a person can be compassionate" argues for the presence of a deity based on the capacity to know according to the object; furthermore, water is insentient yet can moisten what lies below. In what way does its moistening according to the vessel differ from compassionate thought? In what way does its conforming to the squareness or roundness of the vessel differ from conforming to the nature of the object?
If humans possess a spirit, then water should also possess one;
if it is claimed that water lacks a spirit, then humans should likewise lack one.
Therefore, it is said: "You are also like this."

Regarding the examination of "water" by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): to say it exists, to say it does not exist, to say both, or to say neither—all these are forms of abiding. Only when one does not give rise to these four attachments is it called "non-abiding.

As for the texts examining the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that all cite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samantabhadra-paripṛcchā*, this refers to the passage in that sutra where Śāriputra explains to Upāsena that the four great elements have no master, and that the two [senses] enter into the limit of reality (*yathābhūta*).
That [text] also belongs to the Mahāyāna, and its intent is the same as this one.
A detailed explanation of that sūtra’s refutation of the four great elements is found in the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation), within the section on "Following One's Own Intent.
Second, a general examination.
Regarding the statement, “In general, it is said that there is no self with reference to the four great elements,” Jingxi says:
Question: Why does he not say ‘by way of analogy’ (譬) but rather ‘with reference to’ (約)?
Answer: ‘With reference to’ (約) means ‘relying upon for establishment. Because one relies on the external to refute the internal, he simply uses the term ‘with reference to.’
Now, by inferring from external objects up to those that have no owner, one knows that the body has no owner.
Because one knows the internal by means of the external, it is said "by means of" (*yao*). The remaining elements (*mahābhūta*) should be understood accordingly.

The external claim that there is a soul upon which the body depends, and the internal claim that this body depends on the great elements (*mahābhūta*), both regard the great elements in relation to the body; yet for the great elements, the great elements themselves are real dharmas.
The externalist is deluded regarding this and asserts the existence of a soul and so forth.
The four great elements are not one; upon whom, then, does the spirit depend?
If it depends upon all four together, there should be four selves.

The commentary states "four bodies," which precisely refutes the notion of four selves; because the self depends on the body, it is called "four selves," as both the internal and external possess the four great elements.

As stated in the "Preface to the Four-Part Vinaya" (*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*): "And those who have realized it through bodily witness.
Lately, in copying and discussing this text, many have habitually changed the character "yǐ" (by/with) to "yǔ" (and/with).

Regarding the statement, "Even grasses, trees, tiles, and rubble undergo transformation through yin and yang": grasses and trees flourish in spring and wither in autumn; tiles and rubble become damp at their bases when rain is imminent—all of these appear as if they possess sentience.

These four are precisely the four among the ten perceptions.

First, regarding the perception of impurity: within the bodies of oneself and others there are thirty-six impure substances; externally, foul secretions constantly flow from the nine orifices. From birth until death, there is not a single thing that is pure.
Regarding the second, "impurity of food": one contemplates that all food and drink are impure, existing solely due to impure causes and conditions.

2. Regarding the four types of suffering, there are two parts;
first, the actual presentation.
As for the passage from "Furthermore" up to "constituting the four sufferings," Jingxi says:
It need not be restricted solely to the four foundations of mindfulness, because the contemplation of impermanence also penetrates the path of cultivation.

Although they are exempt from the four miserable realms, they still undergo seven rounds of birth and so forth among humans and devas; how much more so when they continue to come and go between the human and deva realms of the desire realm, which can likewise be considered in terms of birth and so forth.
2. From "But only four" onwards is the concluding judgment. Jingxi says:

This is because when practicing contemplation, one contemplates the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*); since these afflictions of thought belong to the category of phenomena (*vastu*), they are referred to as "phenomena."
Now, principle and phenomenon are also called the universal and the particular, or the subtle and the coarse.
Principle is universal while phenomena are particular; principle is subtle while phenomena are coarse.
When principle is contrasted with the coarse, this principle remains a phenomenon.

Regarding the "five kinds of impurity": first is impurity of the seed, because this body gathers up the discarded remains of another and entrusts consciousness to dwell within them.
Second, impurity of dwelling place: for ten months one dwells between the mother’s receptacle of the raw (āma) and the cooked (pakva), and upon birth, one emerges through the urinary tract.
Third, impurity of intrinsic nature: while lying in sleep, one is defiled by excrement, and the nine orifices constantly discharge fluids.
Fourth is impurity by nature, because within the body there is nothing but urine, pus, and blood.
Fifth is ultimate impurity, because at the end of life, when the body decays, its stench is even more foul than that of a dead dog.
This is explained in detail in the seventh fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*. Jingxi states:

Therefore, one should know that it also pertains to birth.
Regarding the phrase "even though one bathes," some say:

Regarding the phrase "mountains, seas, space, and markets," the second fascicle of the *Dharmapada-sūtra* states: "There were four brothers who were brahmins; each had attained supernatural powers and knew that they would all die seven days hence. They consulted together on how to escape."
One said: "I shall enter the great ocean, neither reaching the ground below nor emerging from the water above.
Another said:
"Entering the belly of Mount Sumeru, he returns and joins with the mountain.
Another version says:

One said, "Enter the great marketplace.
Each then spoke:
"By avoiding such places, how could the ghost of Impermanence know our whereabouts?
Having concluded their deliberations, they took leave of the king and expressed their intention to depart.

The city superintendent informed the king:

The king said:

When death arrives, it is impossible to avoid; how can this be verified?
The *Book of Jin* states: "Guo Pu was masterful in the arts of Yin-Yang and calendrical calculation.
During the reign of Emperor Yuan of Jin, he was on friendly terms with Huan Yi and would visit him frequently."
When Pu was among the women, he entered.
Pu said, "Since you have come, you may proceed directly elsewhere; however, you must not seek me out in the latrine."
"If you do so, you will surely meet with calamity.

Later, Huiyi, while intoxicated, went to visit Zhiyuan and happened upon him in the latrine; he crept up to observe him and saw him naked, with his hair disheveled, holding a blade in his mouth as he offered libations.
When Pu saw Yi, he struck his heart in great alarm and said,
"I have repeatedly instructed you not to come, yet you have acted contrary to this.
Not only will this bring disaster upon me, but you yourself shall not escape it either."
"Heaven itself has brought this about; whom can one blame?

Thus we know that when retribution is already fixed by karmic response, how could it be reached through prayers for averting disaster?
Yet you say that Heaven truly acts as the agent; how late is your realization!

I address future generations: you should believe what Vimalakīrti has taught, for it is the true method of prayer and ritual appeasement. This is the text from the seventy-fifth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the phrase "fully set forth in the Great Sūtra," this means it clearly explains the snake, the thief, and the empty village.
Thus, the "Chapter on Noble Practices" states: "Suppose there were a king who placed four venomous snakes in a single basket and ordered a man to look after and feed them."
"If you cause even a single snake to become enraged, I shall execute you by the law in the marketplace.
The man was terrified; he abandoned the basket and fled.
The king again dispatched five caṇḍālas who followed him with drawn swords, and he also sent one man to feign friendship.
That man did not trust him and hid himself within a village settlement.
He heard a voice in the air saying,
"Tonight, six great thieves shall come.
The man fled in terror.
On the road, he encountered a river and crossed its current by means of a raft, arriving safely and without harm.

The four snakes symbolize the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); the five *caṇḍālas* symbolize the five aggregates (*skandha*); the one who feigns intimacy symbolizes craving; the empty village symbolizes the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*); the six great thieves symbolize the six external sense objects (*viṣaya*); the river symbolizes afflictions (*kleśa*); the boat and raft symbolize the path of the six perfections and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*); and arriving safely and without harm symbolizes the attainment of Great Nirvāṇa.

Regarding the phrase "this is the Dharma-body": merit and wisdom constitute the five constituents; wisdom (*prajñā*) and knowledge-and-vision belong to wisdom (*jñāna*), while the remaining three belong to merit (*puṇya*).

Regarding the phrase “the distinct and perfect [teachings] manifest the Buddha-nature through merit and wisdom”: merit and wisdom refer to the conditions and the cause. In terms of the horizontal aspect, the conditions and the cause are fully possessed at every stage of cultivation.

This is because the three types of wisdom awaken the three fundamental [natures], and furthermore, the three types of merit assist wisdom to adorn the foundation.

If there are different understandings from a single sound, it is simply that what is seen differs for each of the five [vehicles] within a single teaching.

When the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) speaks of "seeing the Truth" as being "perfectly ultimate," this is not the perfection of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); rather, it is called "perfect" only because it is ultimate.

Regarding the phrase "nine kinds of precepts" and so forth: in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, each of the six perfections contains nine aspects; while the names are identical, their meanings differ. Therefore, the text here employs those three sets of nine from that work to constitute the three divisions.
Regarding the phrase "clearly knowing and seeing the manifestation of the Dharmakāya," this refers solely to the vision of principle (*li*).
Throughout all stages—whether cause or fruit, delusion or awakening—the stage itself possesses both concealment and manifestation.

Regarding the statement in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) that, "for the time being, it is no different from the Separate [Teaching]," the intent is that both reach the same ultimate fruit of eternal abiding; however, there is a great difference in the objects of cultivation, the wisdom, and the cause and effect within the Perfect Teaching.

However, regarding the fact that all three [stages] of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) are said to be "ninefold," this refers collectively to those from the stages prior to the Grounds up to Equal Enlightenment; since their realization of the Path is for the time being the same, it is said that there is no distinction.
From the words "If one wishes to distinguish" onwards, the text further analyzes these distinctions.

Regarding the phrase, "Previously, among the three teachings, there was no principle of practicing the five causes simultaneously," the term "equal in terms of phenomena" (*shìděng*) is used because it employs phenomena to illustrate the principle; thus, it is called "equal in terms of phenomena.
That is to say, the greatness of the Dharmakāya resides within the smallness of the afflictions; since small and great are eternally so, they do not obstruct one another.
Moreover, at the time of the ultimate fruition, the great is always contained within the small; thus, the functions of the causal capacity can place Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed.

Therefore, the statement that there is "no interruption" merely points to the vision of the inconceivable Dharmakāya, fully present within a single, ordinary, base thought-instant (*kṣaṇa*); it does not concern the actual physical interpenetration of phenomena.

Therefore, those within the teachings of the provisional means (upāya) are deluded regarding the inconceivable principle of mutual non-obstruction; even if they hear of the eternal abiding, their understanding of the obstacles and their liberation remains divided. Consequently, for those of expedient capacity, the realization based on these teachings is not yet ultimate. However, once they reach the stages of the Bodhisattva grounds (bhūmi), their superior function is no different from others; thus, divergent interpretations persist within the path of the teachings.
Therefore, in the Perfect Teaching alone, the beginning and the end are identical as one; thus, the fivefold Dharma-body does not deviate from the ordinary physical substance.

Regarding the statement, "The practice of wisdom that contemplates principle is called the Wisdom-body," this refers to the aspect of cultivation through causes, wherein precepts and meditative concentration serve as aids. Consequently, it is said that within the realm of phenomena, the perfection of wisdom encompasses all partial forms of wisdom; therefore, the Perfect Wisdom is established as the True Path.
By employing the primary and auxiliary practices together, there is nowhere they do not harmonize, because the primary and auxiliary are practiced in unison.
Second, the Four Immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).

Now, these four immeasurables should all be categorized according to three types: those conditioned by sentient beings, those conditioned by phenomena (*dharmālambana*), and those without conditions (*anālambana*).

Furthermore, both the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explain [the three types of compassion] based on great compassion (*maitrī*); by comparing great compassion with these three, their meanings can be inferred accordingly.

Now, these four teachings generally take the "conditioning of birth" (*janma-pratyaya*) as their object: the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings reach two of them, while the *Distinct* and *Perfect* teachings possess all three.

Furthermore, although both [the Shared and Distinct/Perfect teachings] observe arising, there is a difference in the breadth or narrowness of their objects: the Shared and the Distinct observe six [realms], while the Perfect observes ten.

In the Shared and the Distinct, one takes emptiness as the extinction of objects, reaching only the stage of conditioned dharmas; within the observation of the Distinct and the Perfect, one cultivates the objectless (anālambana) simultaneously.

Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The object of focus for loving-kindness consists of all sentient beings, regarded as one's parents, wife, children, and relatives; this is called 'the object-condition of sentient beings' (*sattvālambana*)."
"To see that all phenomena arise from conditions is called 'conditioned by dharmas' (dharmālambana).
To dwell neither in the mark of dharmas nor in the mark of sentient beings is called 'unconditioned' (anālambana).

Regarding the phrase "the Tripitaka and Shared [teachings] reach Great Compassion": this means that through the cultivation of causes one attains the fruit; thus, both cause and fruit are characterized by compassion.
The subsequent passages are similar.

Among them, although those of the *Zang* (Hīnayāna) school do not sever delusions, their cultivation of the contemplation of impermanence still belongs to the category of conditioned dharmas (*dharmālambana*).

Although both the *Bié* (Separate) and *Yuán* (Perfect) Teachings possess all three [types of contemplation], in the Separate Teaching, the "objectless" (*anālambana*) contemplation is only attained at the first stage; this differs from the Perfect Teaching, wherein all three are possessed from the very first mind.

Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "If compassion is neither existent nor non-existent, neither being existent nor non-existent, such compassion cannot be conceived by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the like."
"This is precisely the practice cultivated by one who has realized the perfect integration of the three types of loving-kindness as a single entity.
Regarding the phrase "if a beginner," etc., Jingxi states:
"All intended meanings are fully contained within what has been explained above."

This text also speaks by way of general application, hence it says "entering emptiness. One should know that all of these take the compassion based on sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*) as the object of contemplation;

therefore, in each of the preceding teachings, they are all said to be "compassion based on phenomena" (*dharmālambana*). Thus, in the *Tripiṭaka* and *Shared* (Tong) teachings, one reaches only the stage of compassion based on phenomena; in the *Distinct* (Bie) teaching, one only attains "unconditioned" (*anālambana*) compassion at the final stage of the mind; whereas in the *Perfect* (Yuan) teaching, one cultivates the three types of compassion from the very first moment of the mind.

Regarding the phrase "Nanda’s forgetting of attachment": because he employs compassion and perceives others as being freed from suffering and attaining happiness, he gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*) without expecting any reward; this is precisely the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), and thus it is said that he has "forgotten attachment."
Third, the various *pāramitās*.
Regarding the statement, "The four teachings and six *pāramitās* are as previously explained," Jingxi says:
As explained previously in the "Buddha-land" chapter, these are employed as practices for exhorting and seeking; therefore, it must be so.
Regarding the phrase "expanding the six into seven hundred," the number seventy is fully explained as previously noted.

within each of the eleven [categories], they further mutually support one another.

Regarding the phrase "eighty thousand" and so forth: it is said that there are eighty thousand [dharmas] for each of the samādhis, afflictions, and dhāraṇīs; they are so named because all those eighty thousand have reached the other shore.
Regarding "the various pāramitās," it means that through a single practice and a single mind, one reaches the other shore.
Fourth is "expedient means" (*upāya*).
As for the phrase "as previously explained," Jingxi says:

Regarding the "expedient means for producing the dharma-body of the fruition stage," Jingxi says:
This is because they lead through to the ultimate fruit.

Jingxi said: "The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are the fruit, yet they are also said to arise from the six supernormal powers because when one's habitual tendencies have not yet been exhausted, although they are called 'five supernormal powers' in appearance, this is merely a deference to the name of the fruit; in reality, one has already attained the untainted (anāsrava) supernormal powers. Therefore, the six fruits arise from the six causes."
The "Distinct" and "Perfect" [Vehicles] are likewise names borrowed from the fruit;
thus we know that there are also six divisions within the cause that result in the six fruits.
Sixth, the Three Clarities (trividyā).

Regarding the phrase "all are based on the three supernormal knowledges" (*tisro vidyāḥ*) and so forth: among the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), one generates great revulsion toward suffering by perceiving past births through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*); one generates great revulsion toward the suffering of future births by knowing them through the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*); and regarding the present, one is able to practice correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) through the knowledge of the destruction of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*). Therefore, these three supernormal knowledges specifically receive the name "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*).

As for the remaining three, the supernormal power of the body is merely a form of craftsmanship; the divine ear merely hears sounds; and the knowledge of others' minds takes others' distinct thoughts as its object. Therefore, these remaining three are designated merely as "supernormal powers" (abhijñā).
This is as explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

Following the section on "penetrating clarity" (*abhijñā-vidyā*), one should ask: Since these three are designated as both "penetrations" (*abhijñā*) and "knowledges" (*vidyā*), how do these two meanings differ?
Therefore, the present commentary explains:
"To clarify the distinctions" means to explain them comprehensively.

Therefore, Jingxi said:

Furthermore, the inclusion of the Buddha’s majestic deportance (*īryāpatha*) within the factors conducive to the Path (*bodhipakṣadharma*) is precisely their characteristic manifestation.

Regarding the passage "giving up the robes they had been wearing," it refers to how, after those three hundred bhikṣus heard the Prajñāpāramitā in that sūtra, they all offered their saṃghāṭī robes as an act of worship.

with this as the condition, they were permitted to join this assembly. "To hear this teaching" refers to hearing about the Buddha-land.

Regarding the first point, the clarification of the distinction between teacher and disciple, the phrase "the capacity to complete the work of a craftsman" refers to what Master Xunzi said: "Geng Jiang, Mo Ye, Ju Que, and Bi Lu—these were all the fine swords of antiquity."
However, without being whetted and sharpened, it cannot become keen; without the application of human effort, it cannot cut.

Thus, although a person may possess a naturally excellent disposition and a mind endowed with eloquence and wisdom, they must seek out a worthy teacher to serve and choose a virtuous friend to befriend; for "the virtue of what is bestowed" refers to that which is acquired through such resources.
The learner takes the Dharma from the teacher; therefore, they are called "provisional" (zi).
The *Analects* says: "When Zilu heard the Master's words, he was not yet able to put them into practice; his only fear was hearing more."
Below the section "The Meaning of 'Zi'" (資則), the text proceeds to the correct explanation of the disciple (*śiṣya*).
First, the meaning of "son" (*zi*) is explained; second, the meaning of "younger brother" (*di*) is explained.
The reason for using the term "disciple" is that the word "younger brother" manifests the humility of the teacher, while the word "son" demonstrates one's own reverence.
Since both humility and reverence are expressed therein, it is called "disciple" (śiṣya).
Thus, one refers to oneself as a disciple, and the teacher likewise calls one a disciple; therefore, we know that this name contains both humility and reverence.
Regarding the phrase "abandoning one's father to follow a teacher," the Guliang Commentary states: "Duke Zhao of Lu said:
'Once a child is born, that he does not escape the perils of water and fire is the fault of the mother.'"
If a child reaches the age of maturity without having approached a teacher, it is the fault of the father.
If he has approached a teacher, yet his learning lacks direction and his mind does not achieve understanding, it is the fault of the teacher.
"Revering the teacher as a father" means that among the three upon whom human life depends, one serves them all as one; therefore, one reveres the teacher as a father.
"Abiding with resources as a younger brother" means to settle in one's resources according to the conduct of a younger brother toward his elder brothers.
The phrase "Therefore, as for... introduces Confucianism as corroborative evidence.
The *Analects* states: "When Yan Yuan died, his disciples wished to give him a lavish funeral.
The Master said:"
"No. His disciples gave him a lavish burial.
The Master said:
"Hui looked upon me as a father;
I could not look upon him as a son.
It was not my fault; it was those other disciples."
Now, the Great Master has cited this passage, altering the wording so that it may be easily understood.
However, regarding the interpretation of the meaning of "disciple" (śrāvaka), there are two schools of thought.
First, the explanation of Nanshan states:
One is called a "disciple" (*di*) because they dwell behind the teacher in their studies; one is called a "son" (*zi*) because their understanding follows from the teacher.
Second, former scholars explain:
one is called a "disciple" because they serve the teacher with the same etiquette as that shown toward a father or elder brother.
Taken together, these form three explanations, which are like the orchid and the chrysanthemum.
Following the section on "the present body," the text concludes and returns to the main point.
Thus we know that "disciple" (*śrāvaka*) reveals the humility of the Tathāgata, while "son" (*putra*) manifests the reverence of the *śrāvakas*; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Disciples."

Śāriputra then tied a rope to a Jambū tree; when Maudgalyāyana pulled on it, the entire world-system shook, and even the great trichiliocosm could no longer remain standing.
The seats of the Buddhas of the other directions were immediately bound fast, and none throughout the ten directions could be moved.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"My supernatural power is supreme, yet now I cannot move them."
"Will you not lose your supernatural power?
He then urged him to depart.
He replied:
"Go ahead first.
After Maudgalyāyana had returned to the Buddha's presence, he saw Śāriputra already before the Buddha.
Maudgalyāyana reported the matter to the Buddha, as detailed in the commentary.
2. Second, regarding the answer: as for the fact that among these ten qualities some are naturally more predominant, this means that each of the ten individuals possesses all ten qualities in full.
For example, when Maudgalyāyana is compared to Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana’s ten qualities are all inferior, while Śāriputra’s ten qualities are all superior.

However, among his own ten qualities, Śāriputra’s wisdom was the most preeminent, while Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers were the most preeminent among his own ten qualities; therefore, they were named after their most outstanding attribute.
Since both Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were equally eminent, it is not at all surprising that Maudgalyāyana’s supernatural powers were inferior [to Śāriputra’s].
By taking these two as examples, the hierarchy of the other eight can be understood.

Regarding the phrase "the eight ministers each have their own duties," the *Continued History of the Han* states: "Emperor Guangwu further divided the Three Ducal Ministers’ Office (*Sanguocao*) into two offices; one office was charged with recording the annual performance reports of the various provinces and commanderies."

The Changshi Cao was renamed the Licao, which was in charge of selecting officials and overseeing sacrifices; the Hun Cao was in charge of construction projects, salt ponds, and parks; the Ke Cao was in charge of protecting the imperial carriage and receiving the court greetings of the Qiang and Hu peoples; and the Erqianshi Cao was in charge of official memorials and panegyrics.
The central government offices were in charge of water control, fire prevention, and the suppression of thieves and bandits.
The Three Dukes served as the heads of the Six Ministries, together with the two officials—the Grand Secretary (Ling) and the Vice Director (Pu)—who were collectively known as the "Eight Seats.
Thus it is said that each has its own specific domain of responsibility.
Regarding the statement, "Therefore, ten virtues are divided and assigned to each person," a question is raised:
Since Śāriputra’s ten virtues are all preeminent, why does he not alone possess these ten capacities?
Answer: Even when an enlightened ruler governs, there are still no people who are discarded; how much less should there be partiality in the Dharma King’s transformation of the world?
Therefore, each is designated as "foremost" according to their respective strengths.
Thus, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among my disciples, Maudgalyāyana is foremost in the lightness and swiftness of his supernormal powers.
The Buddha praised each of his disciples in this manner.
III. General Discussion of Mental Factors (caitta), in two parts:
First, citing treatises to demonstrate the meaning, in two parts:
First, citing a verse from a treatise to clarify their number.
Jingxi said: "In this context, I have merely listed them according to the old translations.
According to the new translations, they are: feeling, perception, volition, contact, desire, wisdom, mindfulness, attention, resolve, and concentration; these are omnipresent in all states of mind."

Looking at these old names, one might think that "contact" (phassa) is distinguished as "touching-pleasure" (phoṭṭhabba-sukha) and "feeling" (vedanā) as "pain" (dukkha), while all other names remain the same.
However, these two names are merely different in expression while being identical in meaning.
2. From "This penetration" onwards, the meaning is demonstrated by way of the minister and the sovereign.

Regarding the phrase "like ten ministers of a state," the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan), in the entry for Deshan of the Sui dynasty, states: "The dharma of distraction and turmoil is a malady shared by both the monastic and the secular."
Therefore, when governance is burdensome, the state falls into disorder; when the mind is troubled, the intellect falls into disorder.
When water is clear, the fish and stones can be seen; when the spirit is clear, the inverted thoughts can be recognized.
If even those who study clarity and simplicity remain noisy and distracted, how much more so for one in a position of chaotic administration—how could such a person speak of the Way?
2. From "Furthermore" onwards, the section on the teacher and disciple is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the altruistic practice of the teacher and disciple; second, the application of citations as proof.
Regarding the first part, there is the application of citations.
Regarding the phrase "supporting one another until such a state is reached": if a teacher and disciple together practice good or evil, then all subsequent learners will follow them.
This is illustrated by the examples of the former kings and ministers; therefore, it is said, "it is likewise thus."
Next, the scriptural citations are introduced to demonstrate that the King currently possesses the relationship of teacher and disciple.
Second, from "The Buddha for... onwards, there is the formal demonstration of benefiting others.

Regarding "the King’s mental factors (*caitta*) together transform sentient beings": this means causing sentient beings to receive the teachings and practice them, whereby both the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and the mental factors become wholesome.
Below the section "The Arising of Suffering," Jingxi says:

Question: Since both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) require both primary and auxiliary practices, why is it that in the path of seeing one employs primary practice, while in the path of cultivation one employs auxiliary practice?
Answer: There are two meanings to this.
First, by means of the Dharma, one contemplates principle and phenomena in relation to the Dharma to distinguish between the primary and the auxiliary.

Second, regarding the person: having entered the first fruit and attained the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one subsequently cultivates the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*) from that point onward to assist in manifesting the correct principle and accomplish the three subsequent fruits.
Furthermore, regarding the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is the practice of practicing through conduct; hence it is called "conduct-conduct.
Second, entering the path by way of the Dharma-gates has two parts:
first, clarifying that the ten categories of sentient beings are capable of universal penetration.
Regarding the statement, "These ten dharma-gates can lead to Nirvana," Jingxi says:
"The meaning of this is that they are not merely called worldly mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra*); they also constitute the question of the Dharma."

Why is this? If one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is called merely "existence" (*sat*); when reaching the stage of the four types of witheredness, it is called "withered. Within this, feeling, perception, volition, and so forth constitute the dharma-gate of witheredness; prosperity and the "neither-of-the-two" are explained according to this same principle.
In this Vaipulya [teaching], whether gradual or sudden, all are not outside of sensation, perception, and so forth.
The phrase "as if joining" below uses a metaphor to clarify this:
"joining to form a tree trunk" (hebao) metaphorizes the attainment of the Way, while "the tip of a hair" (haomo) metaphorizes the ten mental factors.

First, the Dharma King imparts teachings according to the inclinations [of beings].

Regarding the passage "First, he draws them in with the hook of desire," etc., these ten mental factors further interpenetrate one another; for now, they are explained from the perspective of the common category of desire.
First, one employs the ten worldly mental states of desire, and only thereafter leads them into the ten numerical categories of the Buddha.
Second, from "Now, the Ten" onwards, it clarifies how the disciple accords with their capacity and masters the Dharma.

Regarding the principle that "people gather according to their kind": those who delight in wisdom enjoy associating with Śāriputra; those who delight in supernormal powers enjoy associating with Maudgalyāyana; all other cases should be explained by analogy.
The *Yi* says, "Things of like kind gather together," yet it is changed to "human beings" to accord with the current meaning.

first, clarifying his mastery of the Dharma and his transformation of the assembly.

The mind-king (citta-rāja) perceives the substance of things in a general and immediate manner; therefore, it is said that it "attains real dharmas" (dravya-dharma).

Regarding the phrase "Although the above clarifies," etc., Jingxi says:

The preceding section summarizes ten numerical categories to explain the ten types of people; although for each individual it is briefly stated that they experience withering and flourishing, this actually refers to each person passing through the five flavors. In this context, the primary meaning relies on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which describes the parinirvāṇa between the twin trees. Since nirvāṇa primarily symbolizes causing sentient beings to enter therein, it is said that [the Buddha] "establishes all his children within it and enters it himself."
Regarding the phrase "these ten disciples" and so forth: the Tathāgata enters [this state] with the intention that his disciples shall all likewise enter therein.
This underlying intent from beginning to end also employs the text of the "Lion's Roar" from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.
Siṃhanāda asked, "Who is able to adorn the twin śāla trees?
The Tathāgata answered in succession by naming six individuals, and Siṃhanāda understood each one in turn, saying:
"Only the Tathāgata is truly capable of supreme adornment.
Thus we know that it is only upon attaining the ultimate fruit that one receives the name of "supreme.
One should understand that the disciples merely resemble the Tathāgata, having attained only a small portion of that which is neither withered nor flourishing.
If this is so, it is not only *nirvāṇa* that is called "neither withering nor flourishing"; rather, all teachings on Buddha-nature revealed by the eightfold teaching may be so named.
Whether in practice or realization, all are termed *nirvāṇa* and all are termed "adornment"—this must be understood by reflecting upon the great purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Some say that the formations,

The Buddha said: "There is nothing that is not the correct teaching.

first, it clarifies the reasons for the reduction of four [kings] in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:"
“World-Honored One!
Which bhikṣus are able to adorn the twin śāla trees?
The Buddha named six persons as well as the Tathāgata himself.
The six persons abide in the cause, while the Tathāgata dwells in the fruit; thus, both cause and fruit receive the name "adornment" (*vyūha*).
Since the four virtues are fully present from the beginning to the end of both cause and fruit, the signified meaning is manifest; therefore, it is called "adornment."

Regarding the six individuals, the Sūtra states: "If there are bhikṣus who receive, uphold, read, and recite the twelve divisions of the scriptures, correctly establishing their words and phrases, such bhikṣus are then able to adorn the twin śāla trees."
Siṃhanāda said, "According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, it is the bhikṣu Ānanda.
Having attained the pure divine eye, he pointed to Aniruddha.
Having few desires and being content refers to Mahākāśyapa;
practicing the non-contentious emptiness refers to Subhūti;
skillfully cultivating supernormal powers refers to Maudgalyāyana.
"Attaining great wisdom" refers to Śāriputra.
For each individual, the details are as extensive as those for Ānanda.

Later, when citing those who have realized the fruit, it says: "If there is a bhikṣu who can explain that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, attains the Vajra-samādhi, and is fully endowed with the four virtues and the eight masteries."
In this way, the bhikṣu is most capable of adorning these twin śāla trees;
were he not present, they would not be dignified.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will dwell here permanently.
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas are by nature non-abiding.
Why do you ask for them to abide?"

Although the preceding six individuals were said to possess great learning up to great wisdom, they must necessarily proclaim that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; having already heard and received their predictions at the Lotus Sūtra, it was not that they were unable to speak of this, but rather that they did not yet equal those who have attained the fruit.
Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata is most capable of adornment.

Both those on the path of cause and those who have attained the fruit possess the four virtues; yet because those on the path of cause have only just begun to enter, it is said that "only the Buddha" [possesses them].
Second, from "What" onwards, there is the demonstration that this present sutra possesses ten underlying purports, in two parts:
First, sentient beings turn their backs on their nature and become deluded.
Regarding the phrase "Buddha-nature is perfectly present," it is because the three causes are fully endowed.
From the word "afflictions" downward, they do not know this because of their delusion.
This groups ten numbers together to correspond with the three causes, each according to the convenience of their respective meanings.
If one discusses the essential nature of the principle, however, each and every one possesses all three.
Since mind and matter are already identical, how could they be separated by the categories of the sovereign [mind] and its mental factors?

Even if one has entered reality, as long as ignorance has not yet been destroyed, one remains merely within the stage of skillful means with remainder.
Since this present discussion concerns those who abide in the middle way and have already entered reality, it refers to "fruition."
Those with great capacity receive manifest benefit, whereas those of lesser practice receive only latent assistance; it is from this perspective of intention that such a statement can be made.

Seven, Clarifying the Purification of Buddha-lands, in two parts:
First, the general explanation. Jingxi says:

Regarding the purification of Buddha-lands: purifying the land is precisely the practice of a bodhisattva; other commentaries on this scripture all lack this point, which is why it is here explained from the perspective of provisional practice.
If one has never revealed their original nature and is shown to be of the Hīnayāna,

and is a proponent of actual practice, then because they have not previously established karmic conditions with sentient beings, they must further cultivate the practices of the Pure Land after first receiving their prediction of enlightenment at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

It clarifies that there must be two distinct aspects to the application of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Next, the citation of "having few desires" serves to verify and reveal the fundamental [nature]. Therefore, only by explaining this passage can it be said that it accords with and establishes the Pure Land.

Thus, we know that both Vimalakīrti and his disciples all possess a real fundamental basis; hence, from the words "This is then... onwards, the meaning of the fundamental and the traceable is used in contrast to Vimalakīrti’s fundamental nature to provide the conclusion.
Since antiquity, people have merely uttered words of disparagement and criticism, thereby forever losing the principle of attaining Buddhahood in accordance with the Land of Bliss.
Eighth, the clarification of contemplating the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the statement, "The previous explanations are also contemplations of the mind," this refers specifically to the two passages concerning the third general correspondence and the fourth specific correspondence.

Jingxi said: "Not only do the Buddha and his disciples correspond in meaning to the sovereign mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*), but for all who enter the Way, the sovereign mind and its mental factors are likewise so.

The teaching is fundamentally intended to lead ordinary beings in their cultivation; in this sense, they correspond to the sovereign and its factors, collectively transforming all minds to fully achieve perfect enlightenment."
If one were to correlate these ten numbers with individuals, it would be as already explained in the preceding section;
therefore, they are omitted here. The phrase "identical to Śāriputra" briefly indicates a single person.
Regarding the phrase "In this way, each one," and so forth: this means that [the Buddha] specifically identified with Maudgalyāyana, and even felt his pain as Ānanda’s.
For example, because Śāriputra used his own clarity to understand that of others, it is said, "each one," and so on.
The phrase "all are based on oneself and others" means that the meaning of the transformative mind is similar to the purification of a Buddha-land.

The statement "if one can reach the dwelling in Great Nirvana" should be understood as referring to the stage of abiding in Nirvana through the semblance of true realization via contemplative practice.

Now, as for the statement that "seeing one's nature is immediately entering the Adorned Twin Trees of Partial Truth," this simply means that the three truths within the single mind are called the adornment of the twin trees:
illuminating the True [Truth] adorns the withered; illuminating the Conventional adorns the flourishing; and illuminating the Middle is precisely entering nirvana in the intermediate state.
Furthermore, each of these three truths possesses the attributes of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as the four aspects of impermanence; this is what is meant by "adorned trees.
As for the phrase "how could the commentary exhaust the mind," it is similar to what the *I Ching* says: "Writing does not exhaust speech, and speech does not exhaust intention."

2. Sequential Explanation, in two parts:
First, Vimalakīrti’s silent reflection, in two parts:
First, his own reflection on being bedridden with illness.
Regarding the phrase "contemplating oneself as the dharma-body of liberation, knowledge, and vision," Jingxi says:
"Liberation, knowledge, and vision" refers to realizing that one has personally attained the Dharma.

In the present case, Vimalakīrti has already realized the stage of fruition and dwells in the rank of Equal Enlightenment; since he possesses the three virtues (*triguṇa*), he contemplates himself as benefiting sentient beings through the virtue of liberation, because he reflects upon his own liberation for the sake of others.

Regarding the phrase "to still all weariness and vexation" and so forth: "vexation" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*), while "matters" refers to karma; one must also still these two matters, which are the worldly ailments.
Now, these two matters likewise represent delusion and karma; when object and wisdom are in accord, these two matters will necessarily be stilled.
Why is this so? Because these two kinds of substance are themselves the seeds of the two virtues of *prajñā* (wisdom) and *vimukti* (liberation).
Now, as the transformation of the seeds of the Pure Name becomes manifest, it is termed "resting."
The four lines following "In the Great Sūtra" refer to the "Chapter on Holy Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-parivarta*).
King Ajātaśatru, having committed a heinous crime, developed sores and swellings on his body that prevented him from sleeping in peace; it was for this reason that he uttered these words.
The Tathāgata has exhausted all delusions and karma, which is termed "attaining peaceful sleep.

Thus, this meaning accords somewhat with the "sleeping" (qin) of Vimalakīrti; although there is a slight difference in their respective emphases, they converge before long, and therefore it may be cited as scriptural evidence.
"Having perfected the cultivation of causes" refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), which is the ultimate position of the true cause.

"Harmonizing with light while not sharing in its dust" means that he manifests illness through skillful means (*upāya*), hence it is called "harmonizing with light"; because he is internally free from delusion and karma, he does not share in the dust.
The *Laozi* says: "Harmonize with its light, become one with the dust; it is profound and still, as if perhaps existing.
This refers to harmonizing with light and becoming one with the dust.
Yet, because the wondrous source is unmixed, it is said to be "profound and still, as if perhaps existing."
Now, borrowing these words and adapting them for our own use, we take the phrase "not being mixed with dust" to establish the meaning of the wondrous original state being unmixed.
Regarding the section beginning with "Questioning Vimalakīrti," Jingxi says:
"The intent of the question is simply that one ought to pity others; why then does he think only of himself?"
The meaning of the answer is that this expresses the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Within these three virtues, because the object and wisdom are in union, they are called the *dharmakāya* and *prajñā*.
However, since liberation has not yet fully unfolded, within the context of the meaning of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), one must speak of "mindfulness" (*smṛti*).
Great Compassion is the very mark of liberation; because it relies upon one’s own mindfulness of that [Buddha], it is said to be "entrusted.
Second, regarding the intent of the Buddha’s mindfulness:
as for the phrase "the convergence of the three conditions," Jingxi said:

To the two kinds of causal conditions, the collection of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is added; prior to the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*), only these two were established.

At the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, the Master [Nāgārjuna] relies on the collection of the dharma-realm because it facilitates the interpretation of the chapter and the commentary on the text.

If it were not so, then disciples and bodhisattvas would merely share a single unconditioned causal collection, resulting in a confusion between the great and the small; therefore, following ancient tradition, they are further distinguished into three types.
If that is so, why do you refute others?
Answer: The names are identical but the meanings differ, as has already been explained previously.
2. The Tathāgata sends a question, in two parts:
first, the Buddha knows their thoughts.
Regarding the phrase "the wise person knows wisdom," this means that a person of ultimate fruition-wisdom knows a person of partial true-wisdom.
Using the snake as a metaphor for wisdom, its underlying meaning can thus be understood.
"Only those of the same kind can see it; others are unable to behold it"—this statement appears in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Second, the dispatching of questions, which has two parts:
First, the division of sections.

first, the command to the ten disciples, which has ten sub-sections.
First, the command to Śāriputra, in two parts:
first, the Buddha’s command, in two parts:
first, a brief explanation.
Regarding the phrase "attendant on the left side," the character "left" (左) is an error; it should read "right" (右).

In the Western lands, rulers, fathers, and teachers all face east; thus, the left is north and the right is south. North is the realm of yin, and yin’s stillness represents meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Supernormal powers arise from meditative concentration; therefore, Maudgalyāyana sits on the left.
The south is the direction of yang; yang represents movement and wisdom, therefore Śāriputra sits on the right.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Maudgalyāyana is the Buddha’s disciple on the left side, and Śāriputra is the Buddha’s disciple on the right side."
If that is so, Śāriputra ought to rank below Maudgalyāyana; why then is he called the "foremost"?
Answer: Because in the Western regions the right side is honored, the right side is therefore considered the position of honor.
This is also like how, in this region, the General of the Left occupies the left and the General of the Right occupies the right.
Some say: "In auspicious matters, the left is honored; in inauspicious matters, the right is honored."
The General-in-Chief presides over military strategy and wields the power of execution; therefore, he is treated according to the rites of mourning. How could he be compared to those others?
Answer: Regarding the rituals of the two realms (the secular and the sacred), there are those that correspond in spirit and those that are diametrically opposed.

That he withdrew to sit on one side and then rose from his seat is analogous to the practice in this region where disciples sitting in attendance upon their teacher rise when they wish to inquire further about the fundamentals or request instruction on their studies; this is a profound correspondence.

If this side bares the shoulder to apologize for a transgression while that side bares the shoulder to express reverence; if this region regards the left as superior during auspicious occasions while that region regards the right as superior—these are their differences.
What is there to doubt?
Now Śāriputra resides on the right side, like a general in the world; since his entrusted responsibility is so great, he was the first to be commanded.
Second, the section beginning with "But" provides an extensive explanation, which has two parts:
First, the formal explanation, in two parts:
first, a brief indication of the causes and conditions;
second, from "entrusting" (*tuo*) onwards, a detailed exposition of the five flavors, in two parts:
First, regarding Śāriputra, he was foremost in all five flavors.

As for the phrase "from the time of entering the womb," once he had entered his mother's womb and began to speak through her mouth, his mother’s skill in debate became twice as superior as it was before.
Regarding the phrase "later encountering a Buddha" and so forth: Śāriputra served the brahmin Sañjayin and was able to master his way.

Once his teacher had passed away, he later met Ārāḍa; upon hearing the meaning of the Three Truths, he attained the first fruit of the path (srotāpanna). Thereafter, he went to see the Buddha and subsequently became an arhat.
In the passage beginning with "Therefore, the Great Sūtra," the person who is adorned is clarified. Jingxi says:
Since the Tathāgata therein manifests entry into the Middle, what is the essence of the Middle?

This means that the "extreme" (the limit) is precisely this [the middle]. Therefore, its withered state is itself the adornment of its flourishing; it is because of being withered that its flourishing constitutes an adornment.
Thus, from the Deer Park until the assembly at Prajñā, the disciples' states of withering and flourishing remained separated, for the traces of their transformative activities continued to differ.
2. Regarding the passage beginning with "Some say," the Great Master (Zhiyi) takes this opportunity to refute ancient views.
As for the phrase "merely grasping the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*," Jingxi states:

"When one reaches the time of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the three vehicles are brought into convergence; only when the three are realized as one can the 'edges' be adorned, because through the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, all are fully incorporated into the Middle."

Therefore, reaching Nirvana serves once again to manifest the ultimate destination of the entire dispensation; it is not that one must wait for Nirvana before being able to establish this [teaching] as a solemn edifice.
Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra*’s reference to "harvesting in autumn and storing in winter" is indeed well-founded.
